lessons.d: Church government begins with a claim about Christ, not with a theory of organization.

s.h: The book begins with a person

b.p: The Book of Church Order does not open with courts, officers or procedure. It opens with Jesus Christ, on whose shoulders the government rests, who holds in himself every office of the church, and who rules and teaches his church from his throne through his Word and Spirit by the ministry of men.
That last phrase carries the weight of everything that follows. Ministers are the means through whom a living King acts. They are not successors who hold his place while he is away.

b.q: The Lord Jesus, as King and Head of his church, hath therein appointed a government, in the hand of church officers, distinct from the civil magistrate.
Christ executeth the office of a king, in calling out of the world a people to himself, and giving them officers, laws, and censures, by which he visibly governs them.

b.p: The Preface says Christ has given his church officers, oracles and ordinances, and has ordained in it a system of doctrine, government, discipline and worship, either set down in Scripture or deduced from it by good and necessary inference, with nothing to be added and nothing taken away.

Two consequences follow at once. Church power is service, not invention: all of it is only ministerial and declarative, because Scripture alone is the rule of faith and practice. And no officer may claim authority or titles of spiritual pre-eminence beyond what Scripture uses.

s.h: A strong claim with a careful limit

b.p: The book calls the representative or presbyterian form of government scriptural, and says it is necessary to the perfection of the order of the visible church. It then adds that it is not essential to the church’s existence.

That limit is not politeness. It is why the same book can recognise other denominations as true branches of the church of Jesus Christ wherever they maintain the Word and Sacraments in their fundamental integrity.

b.n: A church that thinks its order is scriptural, and also thinks a church with weaker order is still a church, is not being inconsistent. It is holding both 1-1 and 1-7.

b.p: Order exists for the sake of the people. Examinations guard who teaches. Sessions give every member named shepherds. Courts above the Session mean no congregation is left alone with its worst moment, and no officer is the last word on his own case.
Read the rules that follow as answers to one question: how are the people Christ has gathered to be taught and governed in faithfulness to him.

qz.q: BCO 1-7 says the presbyterian form of government is
o: essential to the existence of a true church
necessary to the perfection of the church's order, but not essential to its existence
one arrangement among many, with no scriptural warrant
qz.w: The claim is strong about order and deliberately limited about existence, which is why 2-2 can recognise other bodies as true branches.

qz.q: According to the Preface, what did Christ give his church?
qz.w: The Preface lists officers, oracles and ordinances, along with a system of doctrine, government, discipline and worship.

qz.q: Calling church power ministerial and declarative means that a church court
o: may make new laws binding the conscience
declares and applies the law of Christ found in Scripture
may overrule Scripture in hard cases
has no real authority at all
qz.w: Courts may frame symbols of faith, testify against error and decide cases of conscience, but they can make no laws binding the conscience.

lessons.d: Four standing answers to the question of who governs, and where the Presbyterian answer differs.

b.p: Every church answers a practical question: when a decision has to be made, who decides, and who may review it. The historic answers fall into a small number of families.

l: Episcopal. Authority runs through bishops, understood as an order above presbyters. Ordination and oversight belong to the bishop, and congregations are governed through him.
Single-elder congregational. The congregation holds final authority and is led by one pastor, with deacons serving. Associations of churches are voluntary and advisory.
Plural-elder congregational. The congregation still holds final authority, but is led by a plurality of elders rather than a single pastor.
Presbyterian. The people elect elders; the elders govern jointly in courts; and the courts are connected, so that a lower court is subject to review by a higher one.

b.p: A fourth question cuts across all of them: does the civil power govern the church. The Westminster Confession as received in the PCA answers no.

b.q: Civil magistrates may not assume to themselves the administration of the Word and sacraments; or the power of the keys of the kingdom of heaven; or, in the least, interfere in matters of faith.

b.p: Against episcopal government, the book teaches that bishop, pastor, presbyter, elder and teacher name one office and not different grades, and that ordination is ordinarily the act of a court rather than of a man.

Against congregational government, the book lodges jurisdiction in the Session rather than in the congregation, and makes every court answerable upward. The congregation’s own power is real but defined: it elects officers, calls its pastor, and acts on its property.

b.n: Presbyterian government is not congregational government with elders added, and it is not a mild episcopacy. The difference in both directions is jurisdiction: who may judge, and who may review the judgment.

qz.q: The sharpest structural difference between presbyterian and congregational government is
o: whether the congregation elects its officers
whether a lower court is subject to review and control by a higher court
whether the pastor preaches every week
qz.w: Congregational churches elect officers too. The dividing line is that in presbyterian government the courts are connected and reviewable.

qz.q: Against episcopal government, the book holds that
o: bishops are a higher order than presbyters
bishop, pastor and elder name one office
qz.w: BCO 8-1 says these titles describe the various duties of one office and do not indicate grades.

qz.q: In the PCA text of the Confession, the civil magistrate may
o: administer the sacraments in an emergency
protect the church without preferring one denomination over another
appoint elders in a vacant church
qz.w: The American revision removed the magistrate from ecclesiastical matters and left him the duty of protection without preference.

lessons.d: Six features that make a church presbyterian, each with the section of the book that carries it.

b.p: Christ alone is Head. The church has no other, and every officer acts under his law.
Plurality. Jurisdiction is not a several but a joint power, exercised by presbyters in courts. One elder alone is not a court, and a church with only one ruling elder and no pastor has no Session.

Parity. Elders hold one office. Ruling elders have the same authority and the same eligibility to office in the courts as teaching elders, and every court is a presbytery in the sense that it is made up only of presbyters.
Representation. The people elect those who rule. No man may be placed over a church in any office without the election, or at least the consent, of that church.

Connection. Courts are graded, each with exclusive original jurisdiction over what belongs to it, and each subject to review and control above. The courts are not separate tribunals: every act of jurisdiction is the act of the whole church through the appropriate organ.
Spiritual power only. Church courts are wholly distinct from the civil magistracy, have no jurisdiction in political or civil affairs, and can impose no temporal penalty.

Each mark limits a different danger. Plurality limits the man who would rule alone. Representation limits the court that would rule without the people. Connection limits the congregation that would answer to no one. Spiritual power limits the church that would reach for the sword.

b.n: Where elders differ: some hold that Scripture prescribes this order by divine right in every detail, others that it is the best reading of Scripture while leaving more room in the details. The book itself calls the form scriptural and stops short of calling it essential to the church’s existence.

qz.q: A church has a pastor and one ruling elder. The ruling elder alone
o: is a Session with the pastor absent
does not constitute a Session, but takes spiritual oversight and reports to presbytery
qz.w: With one ruling elder and no pastor there is no Session. He is to give oversight, represent the church at presbytery, grant letters and report matters needing a court.

qz.q: Which sentence states the connectional principle?
o: Each court is independent within its sphere
Every act of jurisdiction is the act of the whole church performed through the appropriate organ
Higher courts may not review lower courts
Only the General Assembly exercises jurisdiction
qz.w: BCO 11-4 denies that the courts are separate and independent tribunals.

qz.q: The power exercised by the people, according to BCO 3-1, extends to
o: the choice of officers Christ has appointed
qz.w: Power vests in the whole body, and the people’s part in it is the choice of officers.

lessons.t: How This Book Came To Be
lessons.d: A line from Geneva and Scotland through Westminster and colonial Philadelphia to Birmingham in 1973.

b.p: Geneva, 1541. Calvin’s Ecclesiastical Ordinances set out four orders of ministry, pastors, doctors, elders and deacons, with a consistory of ministers and elders for discipline.

Scotland, 1560 and 1578. The First Book of Discipline and then the Second Book of Discipline, associated with Andrew Melville, set the parity of ministers, rule by elders in graded assemblies, and the independence of the church’s government from the crown.
Westminster, the 1640s. The Assembly produced a Form of Presbyterial Church-Government and a Directory for Public Worship alongside the Confession of 1646 and the Catechisms of 1647.
1706. The first presbytery in the colonies was organised at Philadelphia with Francis Makemie. The exact date cannot be fixed because the first leaf of its minutes is lost.
1716 or 1717. The first synod. Archives differ: the Presbyterian Historical Society dates its creation to 1716, and the PCA Historical Center to 1717.

1729. The Adopting Act. The synod received the Westminster Confession and Catechisms as its standards in all essential and necessary articles, and left the presbytery to judge differences over interpretation.
The 1740s and 1758. The Old Side and New Side divided over revival and ministerial standards, and reunited in 1758.

1788 and 1789. A constitution was adopted, the Presbyterian Church in the United States of America was formed, and the Confession was revised at 20.4, 23.3 and 31.2, which removed the civil magistrate from ecclesiastical matters. The first General Assembly met in 1789.

1861. On December 4 the Southern church was organised, later named the Presbyterian Church in the United States. 1936: the Orthodox Presbyterian Church was formed in June, called the Presbyterian Church of America until 1939.

On December 4 to 7, 1973, at Briarwood Presbyterian Church in Birmingham, Alabama, elders representing about 260 congregations with over 41,000 communicant members organised the National Presbyterian Church. The founding date was chosen to match the Southern church’s own founding date in 1861.
The name was changed to Presbyterian Church in America in 1974, at the second Assembly at Macon, Georgia. In 1982 the Reformed Presbyterian Church, Evangelical Synod joined the church.

The church reported for 2025: 87 presbyteries, 1,673 churches and 286 mission churches, 5,388 teaching elders, 317,773 communicant members, and a total membership of 405,634 counting communicants, non-communicants and teaching elders.

Much of the wording in this book is older than the denomination that uses it. The optional forms printed at the back come from the Southern church’s book of 1893 and the Orthodox Presbyterian book of 1940, which is a small sign of a long inheritance.

qz.q: The first General Assembly of the church now called the PCA met
o: at Briarwood Presbyterian Church, Birmingham, in December 1973
qz.w: It met December 4 to 7, 1973, and the second Assembly met at Macon in September 1974, where the present name was taken.

qz.q: The 1788 American revision of the Confession touched
o: the civil magistrate's place in church matters
qz.w: Chapters 20.4, 23.3 and 31.2 were revised, which removed the state from ecclesiastical matters.

qz.q: Which body joined the PCA in 1982?
o: The Reformed Presbyterian Church, Evangelical Synod
qz.w: The RPCES joined in 1982.

lessons.d: Before there are church courts there is a people who must be taught, and elders who must judge.

s.h: Teaching is not optional to the covenant

b.p: Israel is a people brought into life with God and then taught how to live before him. Azariah describes the dark alternative in three absences: without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without law. Order fails where teaching fails.

The book keeps the same order. The visible church before the law, under the law and under the gospel is one and the same, which is why the elders of Israel stand behind the ruling elder of a congregation.

Moses cannot carry the people alone. Jethro’s counsel and the appointment of the seventy put judgment in the hands of able men who fear God, and the hardest cases still travel upward. Two features of later polity are already visible: shared rule, and graded review.
The charge given to those judges is a charge about impartiality: hear the small and the great alike, do not be intimidated, and remember that the judgment is God’s. Church courts inherit that charge.

Elders act for the people at the Passover, in covenant renewal, in war, and in disputes at the gate. The office is representative before it is administrative, which is why the book grounds the ruling elder in it rather than in a modern committee.

b.n: The parallel is not an argument that Israel had presbyteries. It is that God has long governed his people through appointed men who judge in his name and answer to him for it.

qz.q: Why does the book connect the ruling elder to the elders of Israel?
o: Because the New Testament never mentions elders
Because the visible church is one and the same in every age, and Christ has furnished men besides ministers with gifts to govern
Because the office is a modern invention
qz.w: BCO 8-9 draws the line from elders of the people under the law to ruling elders in the gospel church, and 2-1 keeps the visible church one across the ages.

qz.q: In Exodus 18 and Deuteronomy 1, the hardest cases are
qz.w: Shared judgment with a route upward for hard cases is the pattern later called graded courts.

lessons.d: In the Gospels the King who governs is the Shepherd who saves, and he gives his church the authority to judge.

s.h: Authority that heals before it commands

b.p: Jesus is not presented as the ablest administrator of an existing religious order. He forgives sins, reveals the Father, gives life, and answers the question of what is lawful by his own authority as Lord of the Sabbath. Church government stands downstream of that.
He also exposes an order that had become unfaithful, where tradition displaced the commandment and position was sought for its own sake. Officers are warned by this, not exempted from it.
To Peter and then to the disciples Jesus gives the keys of the kingdom, and binds and looses through the assembled church. The Confession puts this in the hands of church officers.

b.q: To these officers the keys of the kingdom of heaven are committed; by virtue whereof, they have power, respectively, to retain, and remit sins; to shut that kingdom against the impenitent, both by the Word, and censures; and to open it unto penitent sinners, by the ministry of the gospel; and by absolution from censures, as occasion shall require.

b.p: The steps of Matthew 18 are written into the Rules of Discipline: personal admonition, then one or two witnesses, then the church acting through her court. The steps must be followed in order, and a person wronged may not prosecute a personal offense without first trying the means of reconciliation Christ requires.
The same passage sets the tone: the flock is sought, the little ones are guarded, and forgiveness has no arithmetic limit. Discipline is the work of a shepherd, not of a prosecutor with a caseload.

qz.q: BCO 31-5 requires that a person wronged
o: try the means of reconciliation Christ requires before becoming a prosecutor
forgive and never mention the matter
take the case straight to presbytery
qz.w: A court may still investigate a personal offense as if general when the interest of religion demands it, but the injured party must first take the steps of Matthew 18.

qz.q: The Confession locates the keys of the kingdom in
o: the apostles only, and no successors
qz.w: WCF 30.2 commits the keys to church officers, who shut and open the kingdom by the Word and censures.

lessons.d: Acts and the letters show elders appointed, an assembly deciding, and order given for the sake of life.

b.p: Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in every church; Titus is left to appoint elders in every town. The elders of a single congregation are always plural, and the same men are called elders and overseers in the same breath.
The book reads those titles as the Scriptures use them: as descriptions of the duties of one office rather than as ranks.

s.h: An assembly larger than a congregation

b.p: A dispute at Antioch is not settled at Antioch. It goes to the apostles and elders at Jerusalem, the assembly deliberates, its decision is sent to the churches, and the churches are strengthened by it. The Confession takes Acts 15 as warrant for assemblies commonly called synods or councils.

b.q: For the better government, and further edification of the church, there ought to be such assemblies as are commonly called synods or councils.

b.p: The same chapter sets the limits that the book keeps: such assemblies determine controversies of faith ministerially, may err, and are to handle nothing but what is ecclesiastical.

s.h: Order for the sake of life

b.p: Deacons appear where the care of widows threatened the ministry of the Word, and the apostles refuse to abandon either duty. Qualifications for overseers and deacons are written down. Gifts are given with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. A congregation in disorder is told to let all things be done decently and in order.
The risen Lord then addresses churches directly, commending, rebuking and calling to repentance. Officers who hear those letters learn that the Lord judges the institution as well as those inside it.

qz.q: The Confession cites Acts 15 in support of
o: assemblies commonly called synods or councils
the office of bishop over presbyters
qz.w: WCF 31.1 rests the case for such assemblies on the pattern of Acts 15, with its proof texts drawn from that chapter.

qz.q: According to WCF 31.4, synods and councils are to
o: decide civil matters when the state asks for help only
handle nothing but what is ecclesiastical, apart from humble petition in extraordinary cases or advice when required by the magistrate
advise on any public question they choose
stay silent on immorality outside the church
qz.w: This is the confessional root of what is often called the spirituality of the church, and it stands behind BCO 11-1.

qz.q: 1 Timothy 4:14 speaks of a gift given with the laying on of hands of
qz.w: Ordination in this book is ordinarily the act of a court, with prayer and the laying on of hands.

lessons.d: Eight principles stand in front of the Form of Government and set the spirit in which its rules are read.

l: 1. God alone is Lord of the conscience. It is left free from doctrines and commandments of men that are contrary to the Word, or that in matters of faith and worship are not governed by the Word. The right of private judgment in religion is universal and inalienable, and no religious constitution should be supported by the civil power beyond the protection given equally to all.

2. Every church, or union of churches, may declare its own terms of admission, the qualifications of its ministers and members, and its whole internal government. It may err by making those terms too lax or too narrow, but in doing so it misuses its own liberty rather than infringing the liberty of others.

3. Christ has appointed officers not only to preach and administer the sacraments but to exercise discipline, for the preservation of both truth and duty. Officers, and the whole church in whose name they act, must censure or cast out the erroneous and scandalous, keeping the rules of the Word in every case.
4. Godliness is founded on truth, and a test of truth is its power to promote holiness. Faith and practice, truth and duty, are inseparably joined.

5. Those admitted as teachers must be sound in the faith, yet there are truths and forms about which men of good character and principles may differ. In these, private Christians and churches owe one another mutual forbearance.

6. Scripture lays down the character, qualifications, authority and manner of investiture of church officers, but the power to elect persons to the exercise of authority in a particular society rests in that society.

7. All church power, whether exercised by the body in general or by representation, is only ministerial and declarative, since Scripture is the only rule of faith and practice. No church judicatory may make laws to bind the conscience. All courts may err, yet it rests on them to uphold the laws of Scripture.

8. Ecclesiastical discipline is purely moral or spiritual and carries no civil effect. Its force comes only from its own justice, the approval of an impartial public, and the countenance and blessing of the great Head of the church.

b.p: The section closes by saying that where these principles are steadily held, the vigour and strictness of government and discipline, applied with pastoral prudence and Christian love, will serve the glory and wellbeing of the church.

Principle 5 stands behind the stated differences a court may allow at licensure and ordination. Principle 6 stands behind congregational elections. Principle 7 limits what an Assembly deliverance can claim. Principle 8 explains why a church court can only admonish, suspend, depose and excommunicate, and can never fine or imprison.

b.q: God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are, in anything, contrary to his Word; or beside it, if matters of faith, or worship.

b.n: These principles descend from the constitution adopted by American Presbyterians in 1788. The line of descent is standard in the histories and was not checked against the 1788 text here.

qz.q: Which principle holds that a church may set its own terms of admission, and may err in doing so without infringing anyone else’s liberty?
qz.w: Principle 2 grants the liberty and names the misuse of it in the same breath.

qz.q: The principle that no judicatory may make laws binding the conscience is
qz.w: Principle 7 states that all church power is only ministerial and declarative.

qz.q: Principle 8 explains why church discipline
o: carries civil penalties in some states
has force only from its justice, public approval and Christ's blessing
requires the consent of the magistrate
qz.w: Discipline is purely moral or spiritual and is attended with no civil effects.

lessons.d: Two documents make the Constitution, and not everything printed with them is part of it.

b.p: The Constitution is subject and subordinate to the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, the inerrant Word of God. It consists of the doctrinal standards, that is the Westminster Confession of Faith with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, together with the Book of Church Order, which comprises the Form of Government, the Rules of Discipline and the Directory for Worship.

s.h: What is printed but not constitutional

b.p: The appendices, which include suggested forms for marriages, funerals, discipline and terms of call, carry no constitutional authority and are printed for information. The Rules of Assembly Operations govern how the Assembly does its business and are likewise not part of the Constitution.

The Directory for Worship is a special case. A statement adopted by the third General Assembly calls it an approved guide, to be taken seriously as the mind of the church, which does not have the force of law and is not obligatory in all its parts. Chapters 56, 57 and 58 were later given full constitutional authority, and so was section 59-3.

b.n: So a Session that departs from chapter 51 on music is exercising liberty within a guide. A minister who departs from 59-3 on marriage is departing from the Constitution.

b.p: Deliverances, resolutions, overtures and judicial decisions of the Assembly are to be given due and serious consideration by the church and its lower courts. Judicial decisions bind the parties directly involved, and may be appealed to in later similar cases as to any principle decided.

b.q: All synods or councils, since the apostles’ times, whether general or particular, may err; and many have erred. Therefore they are not to be made the rule of faith, or practice; but to be used as a help in both.

s.h: How judges are told to read it

b.p: The standards of review say plainly that Scripture is the supreme judge, that this Constitution is subordinate and fallible, and that it has nonetheless been adopted by the church. The purpose of the standards is to keep the Constitution from being amended, violated or disregarded in judicial process.

terms: Directory for the Worship of God

qz.q: Which of these is part of the Constitution?
o: Appendix J, the sample terms of call
qz.w: The Constitution is the Confession and Catechisms with the Book of Church Order. Appendices and Assembly rules are printed alongside it.

qz.q: Which parts of the Directory for Worship carry full constitutional authority?
qz.w: The rest is an approved guide, taken seriously as the mind of the church but without the force of law.

qz.q: A judicial decision of the Assembly
o: binds only the parties and may be cited later as to the principle decided
binds every session in every future case absolutely
has no weight beyond the case
may be set aside by a session at will
qz.w: BCO 14-7 states both the binding effect on the parties and the use of decided principles in later similar cases.

lessons.d: Power that is real, spiritual, joint when it judges, and only ministerial when it speaks.

s.h: Where it rests, and in what two forms

b.p: The power Christ committed to his church vests in the whole body, rulers and ruled, which makes the church a spiritual commonwealth. As exercised by the people, that power extends to the choice of officers.

Officers exercise power in two ways. Severally, in preaching, administering the sacraments, reproving the erring, visiting the sick and comforting the afflicted, which is the power of order. Jointly, in church courts, after the form of judgment, which is the power of jurisdiction.

b.n: An elder visiting a home is exercising the power of order. Only a court can suspend anyone from the Sacraments, receive a member, or judge a case. Confusing the two is the most common error in practice.

s.h: What courts may and may not do

b.p: Courts may frame symbols of faith, bear testimony against error in doctrine and immorality in practice, within or without the church, and decide cases of conscience. They may establish rules for government, discipline, worship and the church’s extension, which must agree with the doctrines of Scripture, with only the circumstantial details left to Christian prudence and wisdom. They may require obedience to the laws of Christ, admitting the qualified and excluding the disobedient and disorderly.
They may not make laws binding the conscience, and the highest censure their authority reaches is to cut off the contumacious and impenitent from the congregation of believers.

b.q: There are some circumstances concerning the worship of God, and government of the church, common to human actions and societies, which are to be ordered by the light of nature, and Christian prudence, according to the general rules of the Word, which are always to be observed.

b.p: The sole functions of the church, as a kingdom distinct from the civil commonwealth, are to proclaim, to administer and to enforce the law of Christ revealed in Scripture. The power of the church is exclusively spiritual; that of the state includes the exercise of force. The church has no right to construct or modify a government for the state, and the state has no right to frame a creed or polity for the church.
Church courts are altogether distinct from the civil magistracy, have no jurisdiction in political or civil affairs, and have no power to inflict temporal pains and penalties.

b.n: Where elders differ: this teaching is usually called the spirituality of the church, and its application is debated. The text itself both forbids jurisdiction in political and civil affairs and allows courts to bear testimony against immorality within or without the church. Most disagreements are about where that line falls in a given year.

qz.q: Suspending a member from the Lord’s Table is an exercise of
o: the power of order by the pastor
the power of jurisdiction by a court
the deacons' authority over the elements
qz.w: Jurisdiction is a joint power exercised by presbyters in courts, never severally.

qz.q: BCO 11-2 says church courts may establish rules for government and worship, provided that
o: a majority of the congregation agrees
they agree with the doctrines of Scripture, with only circumstantial details left to prudence
qz.w: The Confession says the same thing about circumstances common to human societies.

qz.q: Which statement is true of church courts under BCO 11-1?
o: They may impose fines in serious cases
They have jurisdiction in civil disputes between members
Their authority is in all respects moral or spiritual
They may call on the magistrate to enforce censures
qz.w: They have no power to inflict temporal pains and penalties.

lessons.d: What an officer promises, what the church allows him to differ about, and how that difference is recorded.

b.p: At ordination a minister answers questions put by the presiding minister, and a ruling elder or deacon answers a parallel set before the congregation. The wording is in the book at 21-5 and 24-6 and is not reproduced here.

In substance, each officer affirms that the Scriptures as originally given are the inerrant Word of God and the only infallible rule of faith and practice; that he sincerely receives and adopts the Confession and Catechisms as containing the system of doctrine taught in Scripture, and will on his own initiative make known any later change that puts him out of accord with a fundamental of that system; that he approves the form of government and discipline as conforming to the general principles of biblical polity; and that he promises subjection to his brethren in the Lord.

The minister also answers about his motives in seeking the office, his zeal for the truth and for the church’s purity, peace and unity under opposition, his faithfulness in all his duties, and his willingness to take charge of the particular church calling him. The congregation then answers its own questions, promising to receive the Word from him, to submit to discipline duly exercised, to encourage him, and to maintain him.

The Constitution does not require a candidate to affirm every statement and proposition in the Confession and Catechisms. It is the right and responsibility of the presbytery to determine whether he is out of accord with any fundamental of those standards and so cannot in good faith receive and adopt them as containing the system of doctrine.

The candidate must state the specific instances in which he differs. The court may grant an exception to a difference of doctrine only if in its judgment the difference is not out of accord with any fundamental of the system, because it is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion.
The same requirement follows a minister who transfers from another presbytery or another denomination.

Presbytery minutes record stated differences in the man’s own words, and record which of four findings the court made: that he stated no differences; that the difference is merely semantic; that it is more than semantic but not out of accord with any fundamental; or that it is out of accord, being hostile to the system or striking at the vitals of religion.

b.n: The vow is not a one-time event. An officer promises to bring a later change of view to his court on his own initiative, and at ordination a man is asked whether his views have changed since he was licensed.

qz.q: A presbytery may grant an exception to a stated difference only if
o: the candidate promises never to teach it
the difference is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion
three quarters of the presbytery agree
the difference concerns worship rather than doctrine
qz.w: That is the test in 21-4 for ordination and in 19-2 for licensure.

qz.q: Which finding is not one of the four recorded in presbytery minutes?
o: More than semantic but not out of accord
qz.w: The fourth recorded finding is that the difference is out of accord, that is hostile to the system or striking at the vitals of religion.

qz.q: If a minister’s views change after ordination, the vow requires him to
o: make the change known to his presbytery on his own initiative
qz.w: The second ordination question contains that promise.

lessons.t: The Visible Church and the Particular Church
lessons.d: One church in every age, many congregations, and the jurisdiction lodged in each.

b.p: The church Christ has erected in this world for the gathering and perfecting of the saints is his visible kingdom of grace, one and the same in all ages. Its members are all those in every nation, together with their children, who profess faith in Christ and promise submission to his laws.

b.q: The visible church, which is also catholic or universal under the gospel (not confined to one nation, as before under the law), consists of all those throughout the world that profess the true religion; and of their children.

b.p: Division into denominations obscures the visible unity of the body but does not destroy it. Those that maintain the Word and Sacraments in their fundamental integrity are to be recognised as true branches of the church of Jesus Christ. Dividing into many individual churches follows scriptural example.

b.q: The purest churches under heaven are subject both to mixture and error.

b.p: A particular church is a number of professing Christians, with their children, associated for divine worship and godly living according to the Scriptures, and submitting to the lawful government of Christ’s kingdom. Its officers are its teaching and ruling elders and its deacons. Its jurisdiction, being a joint power, is lodged in the Session.

The ordinances Christ established in his church are prayer; singing praises; reading, expounding and preaching the Word; the Sacraments; public solemn fasting and thanksgiving; catechizing; offerings for the poor and other pious uses; the exercise of discipline; the taking of solemn vows; and ordination to sacred office.

A church without a teaching elder is still to assemble. The Session convenes the people on the Lord’s Day for prayer, praise, the reading and expounding of Scripture, exhortation, or the reading of an approved sermon.

A mission church answers the same description as a particular church, except that it has no permanent governing body and must be governed or supervised by others. Its goal is to mature and be organised as a particular church as soon as that can be done in good order. Its members are members of the Presbyterian Church in America, and it keeps its own rolls of communicant and non-communicant members.

qz.q: Where is the jurisdiction of a particular church lodged?
qz.w: Jurisdiction is a joint power and is lodged in the Session, which consists of the pastor, associate pastors and ruling elders.

qz.q: According to BCO 2-2, other denominations are to be recognised as true branches of the church
o: if they maintain the Word and Sacraments in their fundamental integrity
if they are older than the PCA
qz.w: That test also matters in discipline, at 38-3, when a member joins another body.

qz.q: A mission church differs from a particular church chiefly in that
o: its members are not PCA members
it has no permanent governing body and is supervised by others
it may not celebrate the Sacraments
qz.w: Its goal is organisation as a particular church as soon as this can be done decently and in good order.

lessons.d: Two kinds of member, one covenant, and the vows by which a person enters.

b.p: The children of believers are, through the covenant and by right of birth, non-communing members of the church. They are entitled to baptism and to the pastoral oversight, instruction and government of the church, with a view to their embracing Christ and possessing personally all the benefits of the covenant.

Communing members are those who have professed faith in Christ, have been baptized, and have been admitted by the Session to the Lord’s Table. Only they are entitled to all the rights and privileges of the church, and only they vote.
All baptized persons are entitled to the watchful care, instruction and government of the church, even adults who have made no profession of faith.

No age is fixed for a covenant child’s profession. The time when young persons come to understand the gospel cannot be precisely set, and is left to the prudence of the Session, whose office it is to judge the qualifications of those who apply, after careful examination.

An unbaptized applicant, after satisfying the Session as to knowledge and piety, ordinarily professes faith publicly and is then baptized. A baptized person admitted to the Supper is encouraged to profess publicly, with clear recognition of the relation to the church he already had as a baptized member.
Those received by letter of transfer or by reaffirmation give a testimony of their Christian experience to the Session, and their names are announced to the congregation.

In substance, a person making profession acknowledges himself a sinner in the sight of God, justly deserving his displeasure and without hope except in sovereign mercy; believes in Jesus Christ as the Son of God and Savior of sinners, receiving and resting on him alone for salvation as he is offered in the gospel; resolves and promises, relying on the grace of the Holy Spirit, to live as a follower of Christ; promises to support the church in its worship and work to the best of his ability; and submits to the government and discipline of the church, promising to study its purity and peace.

b.n: The book calls these declarations and promises a solemn covenant with God and his church. Two later provisions lean on them: erasure for willful neglect points back to vows three to five, and every disciplinary case rests on the fact that a member has submitted to the church’s government.

b.p: All baptized persons are subject to the discipline of the church and entitled to its benefits. The nurture of covenant children belongs first to parents, who are responsible to the church for it, and the Session is to establish and control Sunday schools and Bible classes with special reference to the children of the church.

Adult non-communing members who receive the church’s oversight with meekness are entitled to special attention: their rights and privileges under the covenant should be explained frequently and fully, and they should be warned of the danger of neglecting covenant obligations.

qz.q: Children of believers are
o: members of the church by covenant and birth
candidates for membership only after profession
members of no church until baptized as adults
qz.w: BCO 6-1 makes them non-communing members, entitled to baptism, oversight, instruction and government.

qz.q: Who judges when a covenant child may be admitted to the Lord’s Table?
qz.w: No age is fixed; the judgment is left to the prudence of the Session.

qz.q: An associate member may not
o: vote in a congregational meeting or hold office
qz.w: Associate membership is for believers temporarily away from their permanent homes, who keep membership in their home churches.

lessons.d: How names come off a roll, and the difference between pastoral removal and censure.

b.p: A member who moves beyond the bounds of his congregation, so that he can no longer attend its services regularly, has the duty to transfer his membership by a certificate of dismission. Where no Session exists or a certificate cannot be had, another church’s Session may receive him on other satisfactory testimonials and must notify his former church.

The elders of the church he has left are to continue pastoral oversight as far as possible, to tell him of his duty to transfer, and to ask the elders where he now lives to take oversight of him. If after being advised he neglects for one year to transfer, the Session proceeds under 38-4, with allowance for special cases such as servicemen and students.
A member remains under the jurisdiction of the dismissing Session until he is actually received elsewhere, and a certificate of dismission is good testimony of standing for one year.

If a member or officer in good standing joins another branch of the visible church, the irregularity is recorded, the new membership acknowledged, and the name removed. If an investigation or charges are pending, the court of original jurisdiction may keep his name on the roll and conduct the case, or may let him go and, on request, communicate the matters to the receiving body.

If the body he joins is judged by his court to fail to maintain the Word and Sacraments in their fundamental integrity, he is to be warned of his danger. If he persists, his name is erased, and if he is an officer, the authority to exercise his office as derived from this church is withdrawn.

Where a member has willfully neglected the church for a year, or has made known that he does not intend to keep his vows, the Session continues pastoral discipline in the spirit of Galatians 6:1. It reminds him, if possible in person and in writing, of the promises by which he entered a solemn covenant with God and his church, and warns him that his name will be erased if he persists.

After diligent pastoral work, further inquiry and due delay, if the Session judges that he will not fulfil his obligations in this or any other branch of the visible church, it erases his name and notifies him if possible. If the member asks in writing for process, the Session must grant it.

b.n: Erasure is an act of pastoral discipline without process. It is not excommunication, which is a censure imposed after trial on an offender who is incorrigible and contumacious.

b.p: A presbytery dissolving a church gives at least sixty days notice and tells the members of their responsibility to transfer. It may transfer members with their consent and the consent of receiving Sessions, grant letters of dismissal testifying to good standing at the date of dissolution, or place members under a commission acting as a Session for up to a year, renewable.

qz.q: A member moves away, is advised of his duty, and does nothing for a year. The Session
o: leaves the name on the roll indefinitely
qz.w: Special cases such as servicemen and students are excepted.

qz.q: A member in good standing joins an evangelical church of another denomination. The Session should
o: record the irregularity, acknowledge the new membership and remove the name
qz.w: Erasure with warning is for joining a body judged not to maintain the Word and Sacraments in their fundamental integrity.

lessons.d: Which offices continue, how they are classed, and who may hold them.

s.h: Offices that ceased and offices that continue

b.p: Under the New Testament our Lord first gathered his people through extraordinary officers who received extraordinary gifts of the Spirit and were agents by whom God completed his revelation. Such officers and gifts, tied as they were to new revelation, have no successors, since revelation was completed at the close of the apostolic age.

The ordinary and perpetual classes of office are elders and deacons. Within the class of elder are the two orders of teaching elder and ruling elder. The elders jointly have the government and spiritual oversight of the church, including teaching, and only those elders specially gifted, called and trained by God to preach may serve as teaching elders.
The office of deacon is not one of rule but of service, to the physical and spiritual needs of the people. In accord with Scripture these offices are open to men only.

Bishop, pastor, presbyter, elder and teacher are titles that express the various duties of one and the same office. They do not indicate grades. Ruling elders possess the same authority and eligibility to office in the courts of the church as teaching elders, and should cultivate their own aptness to teach the Bible and use every opportunity to do so.
This is why every court is in nature a presbytery: each is composed exclusively of presbyters.

s.h: Titles, and service that is not office

b.p: No officeholder may usurp authority in the church or receive official titles of spiritual pre-eminence except those Scripture employs. Unordained people are not to be referred to as, or given the titles of, the ordained offices of pastor, elder or deacon.

It is often expedient for a Session to select and appoint godly men and women of the congregation to assist the deacons in caring for the sick, widows, orphans, prisoners and others in distress or need. These assistants are not officers of the church and are not subjects for ordination.

b.n: Where elders differ: some describe this arrangement as two offices with two orders of elder, others speak of three offices, distinguishing the minister from the ruling elder. Debate also continues over how far 9-7 reaches and what titles 7-3 permits for staff. The text itself sets two classes, two orders within the first, and one rule about titles.

qz.q: The ordinary and perpetual classes of office are
o: elder and deacon, with two orders of elder
qz.w: BCO 7-2 sets two classes and places teaching and ruling elders as two orders within the class of elder.

qz.q: Assistants appointed under 9-7 are
o: not officers and not subjects for ordination
qz.w: They assist the deacons in caring for those in need, under the Session’s appointment.

qz.q: BCO 7-1 teaches that extraordinary officers
o: have no successors, since revelation was completed
continue only on the mission field
qz.w: Their gifts were tied to the completion of revelation at the close of the apostolic age.

lessons.d: Qualifications, duties, and what is added when an elder is called to preach.

b.p: The office is one of dignity and usefulness. The man who fills it should possess a competency of human learning, be blameless in life, sound in the faith and apt to teach; should show a sobriety and holiness of life becoming the gospel; should conform to the biblical requirement of chastity and sexual purity in his descriptions of himself and in his convictions, character and conduct; should rule his own house well; and should have a good report from those outside the church.

Officers must be above reproach in their walk and Christlike in their character. While they will see spiritual perfection only in glory, they continue in this life to confess and mortify remaining sin. To be qualified they must affirm the sinfulness of fallen desires, affirm the reality and hope of progressive sanctification, and be committed to the pursuit of Spirit-empowered victory over sinful temptations, inclinations and actions.

It belongs to elders, severally and jointly, to watch diligently over the flock committed to their charge, that no corruption of doctrine or morals enter. They exercise government and discipline, and take oversight of the spiritual interests of the particular church and of the church generally when called to it. They visit the people at home, especially the sick; instruct the ignorant; comfort the mourner; nourish and guard the children of the church; set an example by zeal to evangelize the unconverted, to make disciples and to show hospitality; and pray with and for the people, seeking the fruit of the preached Word among them.

When a man is called to labor as a teaching elder, it belongs to his order, besides the functions he shares with all elders, to feed the flock by reading, expounding and preaching the Word, and to administer the Sacraments.

Presbytery may call teaching elders to other needful work, in which case the man must make full proof of his ministry by disseminating the gospel for the church’s edification and must report to presbytery at least once a year.

l: Evangelist: a teaching elder appointed to that work in foreign countries, or where there are no other PCA churches within a reasonable distance, commissioned for a renewable term of twelve months to preach, administer the Sacraments, receive and dismiss members of mission churches, and train potential officers. By separate actions presbytery may in extraordinary situations commission him to examine, ordain and install ruling elders and deacons and to organise churches.

Work outside the church's jurisdiction: allowed at presbytery's discretion, provided the man is engaged in preaching and teaching the Word, presbytery is assured of his full freedom to maintain and teach the church's doctrine, and he reports at least annually.
Chaplain, military or civilian: allowed on the same terms, and chaplains are strongly encouraged to obtain ecclesiastical endorsement from the agency the Assembly authorises.

b.p: As there were under the law elders of the people for its government, so in the gospel church Christ has furnished others besides ministers of the Word with gifts and commission to govern when called to it. These are the ruling elders, and they hold the same authority in the courts as their brethren who preach.

qz.q: A teaching elder commissioned as an evangelist under 8-6 is commissioned for
o: a renewable term of twelve months
as long as the mission church exists
qz.w: By separate actions presbytery may add power to examine, ordain and install officers and to organise churches.

qz.q: Which duty belongs to the order of teaching elder rather than to elders generally?
qz.w: Preaching, reading and expounding the Word and administering the Sacraments are added to what he shares with all elders.

qz.q: BCO 16-4 requires officers to affirm
o: the sinfulness of fallen desires and the hope of progressive sanctification
that temptation is not sin in any sense
that sanctification is complete at conversion
qz.w: It also requires commitment to Spirit-empowered victory over sinful temptations, inclinations and actions.

lessons.d: An office of sympathy and service, with real work and a clear place under the Session.

b.p: The office of deacon is set forth in Scripture as ordinary and perpetual. It is an office of sympathy and service, after the example of the Lord Jesus, and it expresses the communion of saints, especially in their helping one another in time of need.

To this office, which is spiritual in nature, are chosen men of spiritual character, honest repute, exemplary lives, brotherly spirit, warm sympathies and sound judgment, who conform to the biblical requirement of chastity and sexual purity in their descriptions of themselves and in their convictions, character and conduct.

Deacons minister to those in need, the sick, the friendless and any in distress. They develop the grace of liberality in the members, devise effective methods of collecting the gifts of the people, and distribute those gifts to the objects for which they were given. They have the care of the property of the congregation, real and personal, and keep the buildings in proper repair.

In matters of special importance affecting church property they cannot take final action without the approval of the Session and the consent of the congregation. In the discharge of their duties the deacons are under the supervision and authority of the Session. Where deacons cannot be secured, the duties of the office fall to the ruling elders.

The deacons of a particular church are organised as a Board, of which the pastor is an advisory member. The Board elects a chairman, a secretary and a treasurer to whom the funds for current expenses are entrusted. It meets separately at least once a quarter and whenever the Session requests, determines its own quorum, keeps a record of its proceedings and of all funds and their distribution, and submits its minutes to the Session regularly and at other times on request. A joint meeting of Session and Board once a quarter is desirable.

Higher courts may properly appoint deacons to committees, especially as treasurers, and it is suitable that they be made trustees of funds held by church courts. Conferences of deacons may be held, and their actions are advisory only.

b.n: The diaconate is not a board of directors over the congregation, and the Session is not a fundraising committee. Mercy and property sit with the deacons; government, doctrine and discipline sit with the elders; and the Session supervises.

qz.q: Deacons may take final action on a matter of special importance affecting church property
o: only with Session approval and the consent of the congregation
qz.w: BCO 9-2 requires both, and 12-5 gives the Session power to approve actions of special importance affecting property.

qz.q: How often must the Board of Deacons meet separately?
o: At least once a quarter, and whenever the Session requests
qz.w: A joint quarterly meeting with the Session is also desirable.

qz.q: If a church cannot secure deacons,
o: the duties of the office fall to the ruling elders
qz.w: The same rule appears when a church is organised without deacons.

lessons.d: Three marks of a call, and what ordination is and is not.

b.p: Ordinary vocation to office in the church is the calling of God by the Spirit through three things together: the inward testimony of a good conscience, the manifest approbation of God’s people, and the concurring judgment of a lawful court of the church.

The government of the church is by officers gifted to represent Christ, and the right of God’s people to recognise by election those so gifted is inalienable. No man may be placed over a church in any office without the election, or at least the consent, of that church.

God bestows suitable gifts on those he calls. Besides the necessary gifts and abilities, natural and acquired, every man admitted to office must be sound in the faith and godly in life, and every candidate is to be approved by the court that ordains him.

b.n: A man’s own conviction is one leg of three. A congregation’s enthusiasm is another. Neither replaces the examination and judgment of a court, and the court’s approval does not replace the other two.

b.p: Those called to office are inducted by the ordination of a court. Ordination is the authoritative admission of one duly called to an office in the church of God, accompanied with prayer and the laying on of hands, to which it is proper to add the giving of the right hand of fellowship. No man is ordained except to the performance of a definite work.

Ordination of officers is ordinarily by a court, with one exception in the book: ordination by a presbytery’s evangelist acting under the extraordinary powers of 8-6. A Session examines, ordains and installs ruling elders and deacons on their election by the church. A presbytery ordains ministers, and may commit ordination or installation to a commission, though presbytery itself conducts the previous examination.

s.h: Ordination and installation are not the same

b.p: Ordination happens once. Installation sets an ordained man into a particular charge. A ruling elder or deacon released from active duty and later elected again in the same or another church is installed with the omission of ordination, and an ordained minister moving to a new church is installed with a different set of questions from those put at ordination.

Ordination to the offices of ruling elder or deacon is perpetual. Such offices cannot be laid aside at pleasure, and no person can be degraded from either except by deposition after regular trial, though a man may be released from the active duties of his office.

o: inward testimony of conscience, approbation of God's people, and the judgment of a lawful court
inward call, seminary degree and a congregation's vote
a pastor's recommendation, an examination and a majority vote
qz.w: BCO 16-1 holds all three together as the calling of God by the Spirit.

qz.q: No man may be ordained except
o: to the performance of a definite work
with the consent of presbytery and synod
qz.w: Every ecclesiastical office, according to the Scriptures, is a special charge.

qz.w: Ordination to these offices is perpetual, so it is not repeated.

lessons.d: From the first submission of names to the laying on of hands, and how an officer is released.

b.p: At such times as the Session determines, communicant members may submit names to the Session, keeping in mind that each prospective officer should be an active male member who meets the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1. Nominees receive instruction in the qualifications and work of the office.

Each nominee is examined in his Christian experience, especially personal character and family management; his knowledge of Bible content; his knowledge of the system of doctrine, government and discipline contained in the Constitution; the duties of the office; and his willingness to give assent to the ordination questions.

In examining personal character the Session gives specific attention to potential notorious concerns, and careful attention to the man’s practical struggle against sinful actions and against persistent sinful desires. He must give clear testimony of reliance on his union with Christ and its benefits by the Holy Spirit, depending on that work of grace to make progress over sin and to bear fruit. When confessing sins and sinful temptations publicly he must take great care not to make them appear matters of little consequence, but should testify to the Spirit’s work in his progress in holiness.

The Session may render a decision on Christian experience at any point in the process, and on that basis judge a man ineligible for the election, whether he was previously ordained or not. This sentence was amended in 2026.

The Session reports those found eligible to the congregation, giving at least thirty days notice of the time and place of the congregational meeting for elections. If a fourth of those entitled to vote request a meeting to elect additional officers, the Session must call one. The number of officers to be elected is determined by the congregation after hearing the Session’s recommendation.

All communing members in good and regular standing, and no others, may vote. A majority of votes cast, excluding blanks and abstentions, elects. The election may proceed by private ballot without nomination from the floor.

If a large minority is averse to a candidate and cannot be brought to concur, the moderator endeavors to dissuade the majority from pressing the choice; but if the voters are nearly unanimous, or the majority insists on its right to choose its officers, the election stands.

With the Session convened in the presence of the congregation, a sermon is preached, the presiding minister states the warrant and nature of the office with its duties, and puts the questions to the candidate. The congregation then answers its own question, acknowledging and receiving the man and promising him the honour, encouragement and obedience in the Lord that his office entitles him to. He is set apart with prayer and the laying on of the hands of the Session, given the right hand of fellowship, and declared regularly elected, ordained and installed.

A ruling elder or deacon may have reasons he deems valid for being released from the active duties of his office, and the Session, after conference and careful consideration, may accept his resignation and dissolve the official relationship.

An officer chargeable with neither heresy nor immorality may become unacceptable in his official capacity to a majority of the church. The congregation may then take the initiative by majority vote at a regularly called meeting and ask the Session to dissolve the relationship without censure. The Session uses its discretion after conference with him, and reports its action to the congregation. If it fails to report within sixty days of that meeting, or reports that it declined, any member in good standing may complain against the Session.

Where an officer cannot or does not perform the duties of his office for a year, the Session dissolves the relationship and reports the action to the congregation. An officer released for age or infirmity may be designated elder or deacon emeritus at his request and with the Session’s approval, and may attend meetings and take full part in discussion, but may not vote.

b.n: Chapter 24 provides no system of fixed terms or rotation. Where a church uses terms, it is working within 24-7, 24-9 and 24-10 rather than under a provision of the book that creates term eldership.

qz.q: How much notice must a congregation receive before a meeting to elect officers?
qz.w: One week is the general notice for congregational meetings; elections of officers require thirty days.

o: file a complaint against the Session
qz.w: The same remedy applies where the Session reports that it declined to dissolve the relationship.

qz.q: An officer designated emeritus

may attend and take part in discussion, but may not vote

lessons.d: Three courts, one nature, distinct spheres, and a line of review that runs upward.

b.p: The church is governed by various courts in regular gradation, all of which are nevertheless presbyteries, since each is composed exclusively of presbyters. These courts are church Sessions, presbyteries and the General Assembly. The PCA has no synods between presbytery and Assembly.
All church courts are one in nature, constituted of the same elements, possessed inherently of the same kinds of rights and powers, and differ only as the Constitution provides.

The Session exercises jurisdiction over a single church; the presbytery over what is common to the ministers, Sessions and churches within a prescribed district; the General Assembly over such matters as concern the whole church. The jurisdiction of each is limited by the express provisions of the Constitution.

Every court has the right to resolve questions of doctrine and discipline seriously and reasonably proposed, and to maintain truth and righteousness by condemning erroneous opinions and practices that injure the peace, purity or progress of the church. Although each court has exclusive original jurisdiction over matters especially belonging to it, lower courts are subject to the review and control of higher courts in regular gradation.

b.q: These courts are not separate and independent tribunals, but they have a mutual relation, and every act of jurisdiction is the act of the whole Church performed by it through the appropriate organ.

s.h: Moderators, clerks and the ordering of business

b.p: The pastor is moderator of the Session for prudential reasons. A presbytery may elect its moderator at each stated meeting or for a period up to a year. The Assembly chooses its moderator at each stated meeting, and he, or in his absence the last moderator present or the oldest minister longest a member, opens the next meeting with a sermon unless that is impracticable and holds the chair until a new moderator is chosen.

A moderator has all authority necessary to preserve order, to conduct business properly and expeditiously, and to convene and adjourn according to the court’s own ruling. In an emergency he may by circular letter change the time or place of a meeting to which the court stands adjourned, giving reasonable notice.

Each court elects a clerk for a definite period. Besides recording the transactions, the clerk preserves the records carefully and grants extracts whenever properly required, and such extracts under his hand are evidence in any ecclesiastical court. Every meeting of every court opens and closes with prayer.

Original jurisdiction over a minister belongs to the presbytery of which he is a member. Original jurisdiction over other church members belongs to the Session of the church to which they belong. Each rule has one narrow exception, which appears in the chapters on process.

When the proceedings of a lower court are before a higher court, the members of the lower court do not lose their right to sit, deliberate and vote in the higher court, except in cases of appeal or complaint.
