o: may sit and vote on the complaint
may not vote on the complaint
votes only if the Session asks him to
qz.w: Members of a lower court keep their seat above except in cases of appeal or complaint.

qz.q: The courts of the PCA are
o: Session, presbytery and the General Assembly
qz.w: All three are presbyteries in nature, since each is made up only of presbyters.

qz.q: Extracts from a court’s records, signed by the clerk,
o: are evidence in any ecclesiastical court
may be granted only to members
qz.w: The clerk preserves the records and grants extracts whenever properly required.

lessons.d: Who sits, what makes a quorum, who moderates, and the powers by which a congregation is governed.

b.p: The Session consists of the pastor, the associate pastors if there are any, and the ruling elders of the church. Assistant pastors are not members of the Session, though they may be invited to attend and take part in discussion without vote.

l: Four or more ruling elders: the pastor and two ruling elders are a quorum.
Fewer than four ruling elders: the pastor and one ruling elder are a quorum.
No pastor and five or more ruling elders: three are a quorum. Fewer than five: two are a quorum.

One ruling elder and no pastor: he is not a Session. He should take spiritual oversight, represent the church at presbytery, grant letters of dismission, and report to presbytery any matter needing the action of a court.
Any Session may fix its own quorum by majority vote, provided it is not smaller than these.

b.p: The pastor is moderator by virtue of his office. In his absence, if an emergency requires immediate action, the Session may elect one of its members to preside, the quorum then being the same as for a church without a pastor. If prudential reasons make it advisable for another minister to preside, the pastor may, with the Session’s concurrence, invite a minister of the same presbytery.

Where a church has no pastor, the moderator may be a minister appointed by presbytery with the Session’s consent, or one invited by the Session for a particular occasion, or one of the Session’s own members elected to preside. In judicial cases, whether or not the church has a pastor, the Session may elect one of its members to preside, or invite a minister of its presbytery to do so. That provision for judicial cases was amended in 2026.
Associate or assistant pastors may substitute for the pastor as moderator at the discretion of the pastor and Session.
The Session is charged with maintaining the spiritual government of the church. Its powers reach the members, the officers, the property, the meetings of the congregation and the worship of God.

l: Over members: to inquire into knowledge, principles and Christian conduct; to censure the delinquent; to see that parents do not neglect to present their children for baptism; to receive members; to remove them for just cause; and to grant letters of dismissal, which when given to parents always include the names of their non-communing baptized children.

Over officers: to examine, ordain and install ruling elders and deacons on their election by the church, to require them to devote themselves to their work, to examine the records of the deacons, and to approve and adopt the budget.
Over property and meetings: to approve actions of special importance affecting church property, and to call congregational meetings when necessary.

Over teaching and life: to establish and control Sunday schools, Bible classes and all special groups in the church; to promote world missions and obedience to the Great Commission at home and abroad; and to order collections for pious uses.

Over worship: in accordance with the Directory for Worship, authority over the time and place of preaching and of the Sacraments, over all other religious services, over the music, and over the uses of the church building and associated properties; oversight of the singing in public worship; and care that the Word is preached only by men sufficiently qualified; and to assemble the people for worship when there is no minister.
Toward the higher courts: to observe and carry out their lawful injunctions, and to appoint representatives who report on their diligence when they return.

b.p: The Session holds stated meetings at least quarterly. The pastor may convene it whenever he judges it necessary, and must convene it when any two ruling elders ask him to. Where there is no pastor, two ruling elders may convene it. It also meets when presbytery directs. A Session may adopt rules for itself and its committees and commissions on when videoconference or telecommunication arrangements may be used, and how such meetings are conducted.

Every Session keeps an accurate record of its proceedings and submits it at least once a year to the inspection of presbytery. It also keeps accurate records of baptisms, communing members, non-communing members, deaths and dismissions. Meetings open and close with prayer.

qz.q: A church has a pastor and five ruling elders. What is the quorum of its Session?
o: The pastor and one ruling elder
The pastor and two ruling elders
qz.w: With four or more ruling elders the quorum is the pastor and two ruling elders, unless the Session has fixed a larger one.

qz.q: Two ruling elders ask the pastor to convene the Session. He
o: may decline if he judges it unnecessary
must wait for the next stated meeting
qz.w: The pastor has power to convene the Session when he judges it requisite, and shall always convene it when requested by any two ruling elders.

qz.q: Which of these does the Session not do?
o: Examine, ordain and install ruling elders and deacons on their election
Control the music in public worship
qz.w: Ordaining ministers belongs to presbytery.

lessons.d: The court that holds the ministers, receives and dismisses them, and watches over the churches.

b.p: The presbytery consists of all the teaching elders and churches within its bounds that it has accepted. When it meets as a court it comprises all the teaching elders and the ruling elders elected by their Sessions. Each congregation is entitled to two ruling elder representatives for the first 350 communing members or fraction of that number, and one more for each additional 500 or fraction.

A minister holds his membership in the presbytery within whose geographical bounds he resides, unless his presbytery is satisfied with reasons why he should not. Labor outside its bounds or outside its jurisdiction requires the full concurrence of his presbytery and of the presbytery where he labors, if one exists.

A minister continued on the roll without a call to a particular work must make or file a report at least once a year, and may not be so continued for a prolonged period beyond three years without following the procedure of 34-10.

Any three ministers belonging to the presbytery, with at least three ruling elders, meeting at the appointed time and place, are a quorum. A presbytery may fix its own quorum by majority vote at a stated meeting, provided it is not smaller. It may also adopt rules on the use of videoconference and telecommunication arrangements.

Ordinarily only a minister who receives a call to a definite ecclesiastical work within the bounds may be received, except where he is already honorably retired or where the presbytery deems the case necessary, subject to the Assembly’s review.

A minister coming from another PCA presbytery is examined on Christian experience, including personal character and family management, and on his views in theology, the Sacraments and church government. If the examining presbytery does not accept him, it records that fact with its rationale, if one is adopted, and communicates the rationale to his current presbytery. That requirement was added in 2025.

A minister coming from another denomination is examined thoroughly as the trials of 21-4 require, and must answer the ordination questions in the affirmative. In every case the presbytery requires an entering minister to state the specific instances in which he differs with the Confession and Catechisms, and judges those differences by the same test used for candidates.

Before receiving a church into its membership, presbytery designates a commission to meet with the church’s ruling elders to make certain that they understand and can sincerely adopt the doctrines and polity of the church, and in the commission’s presence they answer the ordination questions affirmatively.
Presbytery receives and issues appeals, complaints and references brought before it in an orderly manner, and where a Session cannot exercise its authority it may assume original jurisdiction.

l: To receive candidates under its care; to examine and license candidates; and to receive, dismiss, ordain, install, remove and judge ministers.
To review the records of Sessions, redress what has been done contrary to order, and take effectual care that they observe the Constitution.
To establish the pastoral relation and to dissolve it at the request of either party, or where the interest of religion imperatively demands it.
To set apart evangelists; to require ministers to devote themselves diligently to their calling and to censure the delinquent.
To see that the lawful injunctions of the higher courts are obeyed.

To condemn erroneous opinions that injure the purity or peace of the church; to visit churches to inquire into and redress evils; to unite or divide churches at the request of their members; to form and receive new churches; to take special oversight of churches without pastors; to dissolve churches; and to dismiss churches with their consent.
To devise measures for the church's enlargement within its bounds, and to propose to the Assembly measures of common advantage to the whole church.

b.p: Presbytery meets at least twice a year on its own adjournment. The moderator calls a special meeting at the request or with the concurrence of three teaching elders and three ruling elders from at least three different churches, with notice of not less than ten days stating the purpose, and no other business is transacted. It keeps a full record and sends it to the General Assembly annually for review, reporting the year’s licensures, ordinations, receptions, dismissals, deaths, unions, divisions and new churches.

qz.q: A congregation has 800 communing members. How many ruling elder representatives may it send to presbytery?
qz.w: Two cover the first 350. The remaining 450 are a fraction of 500 and add one more, giving three. The same formula sets representation at the General Assembly.

qz.q: What is the quorum of a presbytery?
o: Three ministers with at least three ruling elders
qz.w: A presbytery may fix a larger quorum for itself by majority vote at a stated meeting.

qz.q: A Session is unable to exercise its authority in a matter. Presbytery
qz.w: This power sits in the opening sentence of 13-9, and there are related routes in 33-1 and 40-5.

lessons.d: The highest court: who sits, what it may do, and how much weight its actions carry.

s.h: What it is and who sits

b.p: The General Assembly is the highest court and represents in one body all the churches. It bears the title of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in America and constitutes the bond of union, peace and correspondence among all its congregations and courts.

It is a permanent court and meets at least annually on its own adjournment. It consists of all teaching elders in good standing with their presbyteries, and of ruling elders elected by their Sessions on the same formula that applies at presbytery: two for the first 350 communing members or fraction, and one more for each additional 500 or fraction. Each commissioner produces credentials before his name is enrolled.
One hundred commissioners, half teaching elders and half ruling elders, from at least a third of the presbyteries, are a quorum.

b.n: Note the difference from many Presbyterian bodies: the Assembly is not a delegated body as to teaching elders. Every teaching elder in good standing may sit and vote.

b.p: The Assembly’s organizing principles state that the church is responsible for the Great Commission, that initiative for it belongs to the church at every court level, and that the Assembly’s committees serve rather than direct the courts, executing policy rather than establishing it.

Its permanent committees are the Administrative Committee, the Committee on Discipleship Ministries, the Committee on Mission to North America, the Committee on Mission to the World, and the Committee on Reformed University Fellowship. A Nominating Committee of one representative from each presbytery presents nominations from slates the presbyteries supply. A six-man Theological Examining Committee examines first and second level administrative officers of committees and agencies in Christian experience, theology, the Sacraments, church government, Bible content, church history and the history of this church.

Business ordinarily reaches the floor through committees of commissioners. The exceptions come directly to the Assembly: the Standing Judicial Commission, the Committee on Constitutional Business, the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records, the Nominating Committee, and ad interim committees.

l: To receive and issue all appeals, references and complaints regularly brought from the lower courts; to bear testimony against error in doctrine and immorality in practice injuriously affecting the church; and to decide in all controversies respecting doctrine and discipline.
To give advice and instruction, in conformity with the Constitution, in all cases submitted to it.
To review the records of the presbyteries, to take care that lower courts observe the Constitution, and to redress what they have done contrary to order.
To erect new presbyteries, and to unite and divide existing ones with their consent.
To institute and superintend the agencies necessary in the general work of evangelization.

To receive other ecclesiastical bodies under its jurisdiction with the consent of three-fourths of the presbyteries, and to correspond and unite with other bodies whose organization conforms to the doctrine and order of this church.
To superintend the affairs of the whole church, and to recommend measures for the promotion of charity, truth and holiness.

b.p: Deliverances, resolutions, overtures and judicial decisions are to be given due and serious consideration by the church and its lower courts when they deliberate on related matters. Judicial decisions are binding and conclusive on the parties directly involved, and may be appealed to in later similar cases as to any principle that was decided.

b.n: An Assembly deliverance is not a new law. The Confession says councils may err, and the Constitution can only be changed by the amending process.

qz.q: Which body’s report comes directly to the floor rather than through a committee of commissioners?
qz.w: So do the Committee on Constitutional Business, the Committee on Review of Presbytery Records, the Nominating Committee and ad interim committees.

qz.q: The quorum of the General Assembly is
o: one hundred commissioners, half teaching and half ruling elders, from at least a third of the presbyteries
qz.w: A special meeting has its own requirements in 14-3.

qz.q: Receiving another denomination under the Assembly’s jurisdiction requires
o: a majority of the Assembly only
the consent of three-fourths of the presbyteries
qz.w: Full organic union is governed separately by 26-5, which requires three-fourths at each of three steps.

lessons.t: Commissions and the Standing Judicial Commission
lessons.d: How a court hands work to a smaller body that can finish it, and how the Assembly tries cases.

b.p: A commission differs from an ordinary committee in that a committee is appointed to examine, consider and report, while a commission is authorized to deliberate upon and conclude the business referred to it. A commission keeps a full record, which is submitted to and entered on the minutes of the appointing court, and every commission of a Session or presbytery submits complete minutes and a report at least once a year.

Where a commission serves as an interim Session, its actions are the actions of a Session and not of a presbytery. A commission of a Session or presbytery is not dismissed before the time for filing a complaint or appeal against its decision has run, and any complaint or appeal filed in time is adjudicated by that commission until the matter is settled by it or by a higher court.

Matters properly executed by commissions include taking testimony in judicial cases, the ordination and installation of ministers, the visitation of parts of the church affected with disorder, and the organization of new churches.

Every commission appointed by a presbytery consists of at least two teaching elders and two ruling elders, and its quorum is one more than half its membership unless the presbytery determines otherwise. Where a commission is clothed with judicial powers, or with power to ordain or install a minister, its quorum is never less than two teaching elders and two ruling elders. Where ordination is committed to a commission, presbytery itself conducts the previous examination.

A presbytery may hear a case itself, with or without process, and may hear references, appeals, complaints, proceedings under 40-5 and requests to assume original jurisdiction. It may also commit such a case to a commission, appointed from members other than those of the Session from which the case comes up. The commission tries the case under the Rules of Discipline and submits a full statement of the case and the judgment rendered. That judgment is the decision of the presbytery.

The Assembly elects a Standing Judicial Commission and commits to it all matters governed by the Rules of Discipline that may come before the Assembly, except the annual review of presbytery records. It has twenty-four members, in four classes of three teaching elders and three ruling elders, each class serving four years, and each Assembly declares the commission as a whole to be its commission. No two members may come from the same presbytery at election, and no member may serve at the same time on a permanent committee of the Assembly.

In the cases committed to it the commission has the judicial powers of the Assembly and follows its judicial procedures. Its decision is the final decision of the Assembly, with no complaint or appeal from it, except as the minority procedure provides. In each case it issues a summary of the facts, a statement of the issues, its judgment and its reasoning, with any concurring or dissenting opinions, all entered on the Assembly’s minutes.

If at least a third of the voting members give written notice within twenty-four hours of adjournment and file a minority decision within twenty days, that decision goes to the Assembly as a minority report, provided both reports were mailed to the clerk of each Session at least thirty days before the Assembly. The Assembly then acts without question, discussion, debate or amendment, on a fixed schedule of thirty minutes for the commission, thirty for the minority and ten for reply. If the Assembly disapproves both proposed decisions, it must set the case for hearing before itself or a special commission, tried on the record.
The Assembly may also direct the commission to retry a case if exceptions are taken on review of its minutes.

qz.q: The difference between a committee and a commission is that a commission
o: may conclude the business referred to it
qz.w: A committee examines, considers and reports; a commission deliberates and concludes.

qz.q: A presbytery commission clothed with judicial powers must have a quorum of at least
o: two teaching elders and two ruling elders
one more than half, whatever the makeup
qz.w: The general rule of one more than half applies to other commissions unless presbytery decides otherwise.

qz.q: A decision of the Standing Judicial Commission is
o: the final decision of the Assembly, apart from the minority procedure
subject to appeal by any member
qz.w: The Assembly may direct a retrial if exceptions are taken when its minutes are reviewed.

lessons.d: Motions, seconds, amendments and the moderator’s chair: the mechanics that keep a meeting fair.

s.h: Why procedure belongs in a polity course

b.p: A court with real authority needs a way of deciding that does not depend on who speaks loudest. Procedure is how a body of equals reaches one decision, keeps a record of it, and protects the member who disagrees. The book gives the moderator all authority necessary for the preservation of order and for the proper and expeditious conduct of business.

The church’s own rules assume a standard parliamentary manual. The Assembly’s rules cite Robert’s Rules of Order Newly Revised by section, use its definition of what is germane, and point commissioners to its counsel on abstaining from a vote on a question of direct personal interest.

s.h: The ordinary path of a question

l: A member obtains the floor from the moderator and makes a motion.
Another member seconds it, which shows that more than one member wants the matter considered.
The moderator states the question, and from that moment the motion belongs to the court and not to its maker.
Debate follows, addressed to the chair rather than to persons, on the question and not on the man.
Amendments may be offered, and an amendment must be germane to the motion it alters.
The moderator puts the question, the vote is taken, and the result is announced and recorded.

b.p: Two common subsidiary motions come up constantly: to amend, and to close debate. In the Assembly’s Overtures Committee the motion to limit or extend debate is not permitted at all, and the previous question, which closes debate, is adopted on three-fourths of the members present and voting.

b.n: A tight rule for closing debate is not a technicality. Every rule that makes it harder to stop debate is a rule that protects the minority, and every rule that makes it easier protects the schedule. Courts choose which risk they prefer.

b.p: Nothing can be done without a quorum, and each court’s quorum is set in the book. Every meeting opens and closes with prayer. The clerk records the transactions, keeps the records safely and grants extracts, which are evidence in any church court. The records go up for review once a year.

Minutes matter more in a connectional church than they do in a club. A higher court reviewing a lower one asks whether the proceedings were correctly recorded, whether they were regular and in accordance with the Constitution, whether they were wise, equitable and suited to promote the welfare of the church, and whether the lawful injunctions of the higher court were obeyed. What was never recorded cannot be defended.

s.h: Where the book overrides the manual

b.p: Parliamentary rules serve the Constitution and never replace it. Where the book fixes a majority, a two-thirds vote or a three-fourths vote, that requirement governs. Where it fixes a notice period, no motion can shorten it. Where it sets an order for a trial, the trial follows that order.

qz.q: In the Assembly’s Overtures Committee, the previous question is adopted by
o: two thirds of those present and voting
three-fourths of the members present and voting
qz.w: That committee is also barred from motions to limit or extend the limits of debate.

qz.q: An amendment must be
o: germane to the motion it alters
submitted in writing a day in advance
qz.w: The Assembly’s rules define germane by reference to the standard manual.

qz.q: When a rule of order conflicts with a requirement of the Book of Church Order,
o: the court may suspend the book by two thirds
the matter goes to the Assembly
qz.w: Parliamentary rules order the business; the Constitution sets what the business may conclude.

lessons.d: A court decides by majority, and the book gives the minority four ways to be heard afterwards.

s.h: Three records a member may enter

b.p: Any member of a court who had a right to vote on a question, and is not satisfied with the action taken, is entitled to have a dissent or protest recorded. Only those who had a right to vote may join in one. A member who had no right to vote on an appeal or complaint may have an objection recorded instead. All three are filed with the clerk within thirty days following the meeting, or with the clerk of the General Assembly before it adjourns.

l: A dissent is a declaration by one or more of a minority that their opinion differs from the majority's action, and may carry the reasons for it.
A protest is a more solemn and formal declaration bearing testimony against what the minority deems an improper or erroneous action, and generally carries reasons.
An objection is the same kind of declaration by a member who could not vote on an appeal or complaint.

b.p: If the paper is couched in temperate language and is respectful to the court, it is recorded. The court may put an answer on the record beside it, and there the matter ends, unless the parties obtain permission to withdraw the paper outright or to amend it.

Dissent and protest put a conviction on the record. A complaint asks a court to change what it did, and can be carried upward if the court denies it. Any communing member in good standing, subject to the court, may complain against any action of it.

b.n: A dissent does not stop the clock on a complaint. A member who wants relief and not only a record must meet the filing periods in chapter 43.

b.p: The Constitution guards the minority in other ways that are easy to miss. A third of the members present when an action was taken can suspend that action while a complaint is pending. A minority of a third on the Standing Judicial Commission can force its decision before the whole Assembly. A large minority in a congregation is given a hearing by the moderator before an election of a pastor or an officer is pressed. And on any question of direct personal interest, the Assembly’s rules point members to abstain.

None of this makes the minority sovereign. A court still decides by majority, and a member who has lost owes the court subjection in the Lord. The point of these provisions is that submission is never asked in exchange for silence.

qz.q: Who may join in a protest?
o: Only those who had a right to vote on the question
Any member of the higher court
qz.w: A member who could not vote on an appeal or complaint may have an objection recorded instead.

qz.q: A dissent, protest or objection must be filed
o: within thirty days following the meeting, or before the Assembly adjourns
qz.w: Filing is with the clerk of the lower court, or with the Assembly’s clerk before adjournment.

qz.q: Which action can suspend a decision while a complaint is pending?
o: A vote of a third of the members present when the action was taken
qz.w: Notice of complaint by itself does not suspend the action complained against.

lessons.t: The Chair, the Record and the Minority
lessons.d: Points of order, appeals from the chair, and why the minutes are where procedure becomes protection.

b.p: A moderator has all authority necessary to preserve order, to conduct business properly and expeditiously, and to convene and adjourn according to the court’s own ruling. The pastor moderates his Session by virtue of his office, and a presbytery or the Assembly elects its moderator.

The chair serves the body rather than leads it. In the Assembly’s own committee rules the chairman may not enter debate or make motions without leaving the chair, and ordinarily does not vote on a question. Members must obtain the floor before speaking or moving, motions must be seconded, and informal discussion of a subject is not permitted.

s.h: Two motions that keep the chair accountable

b.p: A point of order asks the chair to rule that something now happening is out of order. It does not require a second and it interrupts, because it concerns the conduct of business rather than its substance. The chair rules, and states the reason for the ruling.

An appeal from the decision of the chair takes that ruling to the body itself, which decides by vote whether the chair’s ruling stands. Between them, these two motions mean that no moderator has the last word on his own rulings.

b.n: These are the two devices a member reaches for when a meeting is going wrong. Learning them is worth more than learning the whole table of motions, because everything else can wait for the next meeting and these cannot.

b.p: The Assembly’s guidelines for the minutes of a presbytery state the reason plainly. Points of order ruled against by the chair, and appeals from the decision of the chair, whether sustained or lost, together with the reason the chair gave for his ruling, should be entered in the minutes for the sake of any case that may be carried to a higher court, and for the protection of a minority.

That single rule ties this unit to the rest of the course. A higher court reviewing a lower one asks whether the proceedings were correctly recorded, whether they were regular and constitutional, whether they were wise and equitable, and whether its own lawful injunctions were obeyed. An appeal is heard on the Record of the Case and on nothing outside it. A ruling that was never written down cannot be reviewed, and a member who was overruled has nothing to show.
The same instinct runs through the filing periods for a dissent, a protest or an objection: thirty days to put a position on the record, or before the Assembly adjourns.

s.h: A few rules of the Assembly floor

l: Presentations informing the Assembly of the work reported by permanent committees and agencies are limited to fifteen minutes.
Budgets agreed upon by the Administrative Committee may be changed only by a two-thirds vote of commissioners present and voting, and that threshold applies only to changes initiated on the floor.
On a question of direct personal interest, commissioners are pointed to the standard manual's counsel on abstaining.
In the Overtures Committee no motion to limit or extend the limits of debate is permitted, and the previous question carries on three-fourths of the members present and voting.

qz.q: Why do the Assembly’s guidelines want points of order and appeals from the chair recorded?
o: For the sake of any case carried to a higher court, and for the protection of a minority
Because Robert's Rules require verbatim minutes
qz.w: The reason given is the later case and the minority, which is why the guideline asks for the chair’s stated reason as well as the ruling.

qz.q: A member believes the moderator has ruled wrongly. His recourse is
o: a complaint to presbytery at once
an appeal from the decision of the chair, decided by the body
a protest, which ends the matter
qz.w: A complaint lies against an act of the court, and has its own sixty-day period. The immediate remedy in the room is the appeal from the chair.

qz.q: Under the Assembly’s committee rules, a chairman who wants to argue for a motion must
o: ask the moderator of the Assembly
qz.w: He also ordinarily does not vote on a question.

lessons.d: Coming under care, and the licence that lets a man preach before he is ordained.

b.p: A candidate for the ministry is a member of the church in full communion who, believing himself called to preach, submits himself to the care and guidance of a presbytery during his course of study and practical training.

Every applicant puts himself under the care of a presbytery, ordinarily the one with jurisdiction over the church of which he is a member. His Session’s endorsement must be given, with testimonials of his Christian character and promise of usefulness, and should describe the ministry he has taken part in, with a brief evaluation. He must have been a member of the endorsing congregation for at least six months before filing, except where presbytery deems the case extraordinary.

A man may not be received under care and examined for ordination at the same meeting, since he must serve at least a year of internship before ordination. He may, however, be taken under care, licensed to preach and made an intern at the same meeting.

The applicant appears in person and is examined on experiential religion and on his motives for seeking the ministry. If the testimonials and examination are satisfactory, he answers two questions, promising to maintain a becoming Christian character and to be diligent in preparation, and to submit to the proper supervision of presbytery in matters concerning that preparation. He is then given a charge, and his name is placed on the roll of candidates.

A candidate remains a private member of his church under the Session’s jurisdiction, while his preparation is under the oversight of presbytery. Presbytery owes him kindly interest, counsel and guidance about studies and training, and no candidate may omit any subject prescribed as a test for ordination without presbytery’s consent, which must be recorded with its reasons.

He reports to presbytery at least once a year, and presbytery secures an annual report from his instructors on deportment, diligence and progress. He may be dismissed to another presbytery, may withdraw at his own or his Session’s request, and may have his name removed by presbytery for sufficient reasons, which must be recorded and reported to him and his Session.

To preserve the purity of preaching, no man may preach regularly in PCA pulpits without proper licensure from the presbytery with jurisdiction where he will preach. A ruling elder, a candidate, a minister of another denomination or another man may be licensed on giving satisfaction as to his gifts and passing the examination.

The examination covers a statement of his Christian experience and inward call, written or oral at presbytery’s discretion; his basic knowledge of biblical doctrine as outlined in the Confession and Catechisms; his practical knowledge of Bible content; his basic knowledge of the government of this church as defined in the Book of Church Order; oral examination on those views; and a written sermon on an assigned passage, presented orally to presbytery or a committee.

As at ordination, the applicant must state the specific instances in which he differs with the Confession and Catechisms, and an exception may be granted only where the difference is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion. No part of the examination is omitted except in extraordinary cases, and then the reasons and the omitted parts are recorded.

The licentiate answers four questions: on the Scriptures as the inerrant Word and only infallible rule; on receiving and adopting the Confession and Catechisms as containing the system of doctrine; on striving for the purity, peace, unity and edification of the church; and on submitting himself, in the Lord, to the government of that presbytery or of any other into whose bounds he may be called.

A licence expires after four years and may be renewed without further examination if presbytery thinks proper, but the licentiate must apply before it expires. If it lapses, the stated clerk reports the expiration to presbytery and to the man’s Session, and re-licensure follows the full examination. A licence may be terminated at any time by simple majority, with reasons recorded, and becomes void at once if the man’s own presbytery censures him with suspension or deposition or excommunication.

qz.q: How long must an applicant have been a member of the endorsing congregation?
qz.w: Presbytery may deem a case extraordinary and receive him sooner.

qz.q: A man may be taken under care and examined for ordination at the same presbytery meeting.
o: True, if his gifts are evident
False, because at least a year of internship must intervene
False, unless he transfers from another denomination
qz.w: He may, however, be taken under care, licensed and made an intern at one meeting.

qz.q: A licence to preach
o: expires after four years and may be renewed
expires when the man is ordained elsewhere only
lasts until the next stated meeting
qz.w: It may also be terminated at any time by a simple majority with reasons recorded.

lessons.d: A year of tested work, then a call to definite labour before any man is ordained.

b.p: Scripture requires that trial be made of those who are to be ordained, both as to their gifts and as to their ability to rule as teaching elders, so that the office is not degraded and the church can form a better judgment. To provide that trial, a candidate for ordination must serve an internship of at least one year, longer at presbytery’s discretion.

The internship may fall during or after formal theological education, and may run alongside academic work. Its nature is determined by presbytery, but it should involve the man in the full scope of the duties of a regular ministerial calling, and it is both practical instruction and testing, under close supervision.

An intern may chair a Session meeting temporarily if the moderator asks him to, under supervision and subject to being overruled. He is not a member of the Session and does not vote unless he has already been ordained a ruling elder and elected to it. He has the right to conduct funerals. He may not administer the Sacraments.

At the end of the period set, the internship is approved or disapproved. Even when approved, the man cannot be ordained without a call to specific work. If it is disapproved, presbytery may extend it or rescind his intern status. Presbytery may also approve previous equivalent experience by a three-fourths vote at a regular meeting, once its committee reports at least a year of comparable ministry, satisfactory performance of the full scope of ministerial duties, and the manifest approbation of God’s people in a local church.

Before a candidate or licentiate can be ordained he must receive a call to a definite work, ordinarily from a church, a presbytery or the General Assembly of this denomination. If the call comes from another source, presbytery records why it considers the work a valid Christian ministry.

A proper call must be in writing and in the hands of presbytery before it acts. It must include the financial arrangements, such as salary, vacation, insurance and retirement, and an assurance that the work will afford liberty to proclaim and practise fully and freely the whole counsel of God as contained in Scripture and understood in the Westminster Confession.

Every church should be under the pastoral oversight of a minister, and a church without a pastor should seek one without delay. The Session calls a congregational meeting to elect a pulpit committee, which may be drawn from the congregation at large or from the Session as the congregation designates. After consultation the committee recommends a candidate who in its judgment meets the constitutional requirements of the office and is best suited to the congregation’s spiritual interests.

The Session orders a congregational meeting at the regular place of worship, with public notice of time, place and purpose at least one week beforehand. The congregation should elect a minister or ruling elder of this church to preside if that is practicable, and otherwise any male member of the church. All communing members in good and regular standing, and no others, may vote, and a majority of votes cast, excluding blanks and abstentions, elects.

If a large minority is averse to the man who received a majority and cannot be brought to concur, the moderator endeavors to dissuade the majority from prosecuting the call. If the electors are nearly unanimous, or the majority insists on its right, the moderator draws the call in due form, certifies in writing the number who did not concur and any facts of importance, and lays all of it before presbytery with the call.

The call itself follows the form in the book: the congregation declares itself satisfied of the man’s ministerial qualifications, promises him support, encouragement and obedience in the Lord, and obliges itself to the stated maintenance. Commissioners appointed by the church present and prosecute the call before presbytery, which may recommend that they desist, place the call in the man’s hands with or without advice, or decline to place it, as appears most beneficial for the peace and edification of the church at large. No pastor is transferred without his own consent.

qz.q: An intern serving a church may
o: vote in Session as an intern
moderate the Session in his own right
qz.w: He may chair a Session meeting temporarily at the moderator’s request, under supervision, but he is not a member and does not vote.

qz.q: A proper call must include
o: financial arrangements and an assurance of liberty to preach the whole counsel of God
qz.w: It must be written and in presbytery’s hands before presbytery acts on it.

qz.q: Who may vote in the election of a pastor?
o: All communing members in good and regular standing
qz.w: A majority of votes cast, excluding blanks and abstentions, elects.

lessons.d: The examinations that stand between a call and the laying on of hands.

b.p: No minister, licentiate or candidate receives a call from a church except by permission of his presbytery. When a call is presented and found in order, and presbytery deems it for the good of the church, the call is placed in the man’s hands. Ordinarily a man does not move to the field before his examination for licensure or ordination, and an ordained man coming from another presbytery or denomination ordinarily does not move before he is examined and received.

An intern who has completed his internship to presbytery’s satisfaction and accepted a call is to be ordained without delay. No presbytery ordains a man to labour within the bounds of another presbytery; it furnishes testimonials and sends him to submit himself to the presbytery where he expects to work.

An intern applying for ordination presents a diploma from an approved college or university and from an approved theological seminary, or authentic testimonials of a completed course of theological studies, or a certificate from a theological study programme approved by the Assembly and one of the presbyteries. These educational requirements are omitted only in extraordinary cases, and then only by a three-fourths vote, with reasons recorded. He also presents testimonials of a completed and approved internship.

l: A careful examination on his acquaintance with experiential religion, especially personal character and family management, on the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1.
His knowledge of the Greek and Hebrew languages. A presbytery may accept a seminary degree that includes study in the original languages in place of an oral examination in them.
Bible content, theology, the Sacraments, church history, the history of this church, and the principles and rules of its government and discipline.
A thesis on a theological topic assigned by presbytery.
An exegesis on an assigned portion of Scripture, requiring the use of the original languages.
A sermon preached before presbytery or a committee of it.

b.p: No part of the trials is omitted except in extraordinary cases, and then only by a three-fourths approval, with the reasons and the omitted parts recorded. The book warns that these extraordinary clauses are meant for extraordinary circumstances of the church or proven extraordinary gifts of the man, and that presbyteries must neither block a genuinely exceptional candidate nor ordain a man who is inadequately prepared.

In examining character, presbytery gives specific attention to potential notorious concerns and careful attention to the man’s practical struggle against sinful actions and persistent sinful desires, and requires clear testimony of reliance on union with Christ for progress over sin and for fruit. The same paragraph warns against confessing sins publicly in a way that makes them seem matters of little consequence.
The Constitution does not require affirmation of every proposition in the standards, and the presbytery judges any stated difference by the test described in the lesson on subscription.

On the day appointed, ordinarily in the church he is to serve, a sermon is preached, the presiding member recites the proceedings, and the candidate answers the ordination questions. The congregation then answers four questions of its own, professing readiness to receive him, promising to receive the Word from him with meekness and love and to submit to him in the due exercise of discipline, to encourage him, and to continue the maintenance promised.

He kneels, and with prayer and the laying on of the hands of the presbytery he is solemnly set apart. The members give him the right hand of fellowship, the presiding minister declares him regularly elected, ordained and installed, and a charge is given to pastor and congregation. For an assistant pastor only the first seven questions are used, the Session is addressed instead of the congregation, and the word assistant is added in the declaration.

Installing a man already ordained uses three substituted questions: whether he is willing to take charge of the congregation agreeably to his declaration in accepting the call; whether he believes he is influenced by a sincere desire to promote God’s glory and the church’s good; and whether he promises, by the assistance of grace, to discharge all the duties of a pastor and keep a deportment becoming a minister. In ordaining interns as evangelists the eighth question is replaced by an undertaking of the work of an evangelist.

qz.q: Omitting a part of the trials for ordination requires
o: three-fourths approval of presbytery, with reasons recorded
qz.w: The same threshold covers omission of the educational requirements.

qz.q: Which is not among the trials listed in 21-4?
o: A thesis on an assigned theological topic
An exegesis using the original languages
A written examination in church history
A public examination by the congregation
qz.w: The congregation elects and answers its own questions at the service, but the trials belong to presbytery.

qz.q: In the ordination of an assistant pastor
o: only questions one to seven are used, and the Session is addressed
qz.w: The eighth question concerns taking charge of the congregation that called him.

lessons.d: Pastor, associate and assistant, temporary supplies, and how a pastoral relation is dissolved.

b.p: The pastoral relations are pastor, associate pastor and assistant pastor. The pastor and associate pastor are elected by the congregation using the form of call, and because they are elected by the congregation they are members of the Session. An existing assistant pastor may be elected associate pastor on the Session’s recommendation, without the election of a pulpit committee.

An assistant pastor is called by the Session with the permission and approval of presbytery. He is not a member of the Session, though he may be appointed on special occasions to moderate it. The relationship of an associate pastor to the church is determined by the congregation; that of an assistant pastor is determined by the Session. Dissolution of either is governed by chapter 23.

Where changes in a pastorate require it, a temporary relation may be established with a minister called a stated supply. Where no pastor or stated supply can be secured, the Session with presbytery’s approval may establish a temporary relation with a licentiate as student supply, or with a ruling elder supply. Such relations run no longer than one year, renewable at the Session’s request and on presbytery’s review.

When a minister tenders his resignation to presbytery, the presbytery cites the church to appear by its commissioners and show cause why the resignation should or should not be accepted. If the church fails to appear, or if its reasons are deemed insufficient, the resignation is accepted and the relation dissolved. Where a church wishes to be relieved of its pastor, the same procedure is followed.

Whichever party begins, there is always a congregational meeting, called and conducted in the same manner as the call of a pastor. The minister must not physically leave the field until presbytery, or a commission empowered to handle uncontested requests, has dissolved the relation.

Associate and assistant pastors may continue when the senior pastor’s relation is dissolved, but they may not normally succeed him without an intervening term of service in a different field. A congregation may petition presbytery for an exception by a four-fifths majority on secret ballot, and presbytery may grant it by a three-fourths majority. Presbytery is to determine whether the dissolution of the senior pastor’s relationship was brought about in Christian love and good order on the part of those concerned.

Presbytery may designate a minister honorably retired when he wishes to retire by reason of age, or medically disabled when infirmity has ended his active ministry. In either case he continues to hold membership in his presbytery and may serve on committees or commissions if elected or appointed. A congregation that wishes to honour his past labours among them may elect him pastor emeritus.

qz.q: Who calls an assistant pastor?
o: The Session, with presbytery's permission and approval
qz.w: Because he is not elected by the congregation, he is not a member of the Session.

qz.q: An associate pastor succeeding the senior pastor without an intervening field of labour requires
o: four-fifths of the congregation by secret ballot and three-fourths of presbytery
qz.w: Presbytery must also weigh whether the earlier dissolution was brought about in Christian love and good order.

qz.q: A stated supply relation may run for
o: no longer than one year, renewable
as long as the Session wishes
qz.w: Student supply and ruling elder supply are on the same footing.

lessons.d: What a congregation may decide, how a meeting is called, and what makes it valid.

b.p: The congregation consists of all the communing members of a particular church, and they only are entitled to vote.

Its distinctive acts are few and weighty: it elects ruling elders and deacons, elects a pulpit committee, calls a pastor, acts on its property through trustees or corporation officers, and may ask the Session to release an officer.

Whenever it seems for the best interests of the church, the Session calls a congregational meeting and gives public notice of at least one week. No business is transacted except what the notice states.

The Session must always call a meeting when asked in writing by a set proportion of the communing members: a fourth in a church of not more than 100; a fifth in a church of more than 100 and not more than 300; a sixth in a church of more than 300 and not more than 500; a seventh in a church of more than 500 and not more than 700; and 100 members in a church of more than 700.
If on a proper request the Session cannot act, fails to act or refuses to act within thirty days, any member or members in good standing may file a complaint.
The quorum is a fourth of the resident communing members in a church of not more than 100, and a sixth of them in a larger church.

The pastor is moderator of congregational meetings by virtue of his office. If it is impracticable or inexpedient for him to preside, or there is no pastor, the Session appoints one of its number to call the meeting to order and preside until the congregation elects its presiding officer, who may be a minister or ruling elder of this church, or any male member of that particular church.

A clerk is elected to serve for that meeting or a definite period. He keeps correct minutes of the proceedings and business, preserves them in permanent form after they are attested by the moderator and the clerk, and sends a copy to the Session.

b.n: A congregational meeting is not a court. It does not judge cases, receive members, or discipline anyone. Those acts belong to the Session, and the congregation’s remedy against a Session’s act is a complaint, not a vote.
The notice defines the business. A meeting properly called to elect officers cannot be turned into a meeting about the budget or the building.

qz.q: A church has 260 communing members. What proportion must sign a written request to force the Session to call a meeting?
qz.w: A fifth applies to churches of more than 100 and not more than 300.
