lessons.t: Property and the Freedom to Withdraw
lessons.d: The chapter that decides who owns the building, and what a congregation may do with it.

b.p: An unincorporated church may elect trustees with power to buy, sell or mortgage property, to accept and execute deeds, to hold and defend title, and to manage permanent special funds. Such trustees act solely under the instructions of the congregation and may not infringe on the powers of the Session or the Board of Deacons.

Where a church is incorporated, its charter and bylaws must always accord with the Constitution of this church. All communing members on the roll are members of the corporation, and its officers are elected from among them in a regularly constituted congregational meeting. Funds collected for the support and expenses of the church and for its benevolences are controlled and disbursed by the Session and the Board of Deacons as their authorities are defined.

The corporation, through its trustees or officers, or in an unincorporated church those entitled to represent it in matters of real property, has sole title to its property, real, personal or mixed, tangible or intangible, and is sole owner of any equity in real estate or of any fund or property held by or belonging to the church or any group within it. The higher courts may receive money or property from a local church only by its free and voluntary action.

All particular churches are entitled to hold, own and enjoy their own local properties, without any right of reversion whatsoever to any presbytery, General Assembly or any court hereafter created, or to the trustees or officers of such courts.

The provisions of chapter 25 are to be construed as a solemn covenant by which the church as a whole promises never to attempt to secure possession of the property of any congregation against its will, whether or not the congregation stays in this body, and all officers and courts are forbidden to make such an attempt.

A particular church need remain in association with any court of this body only so long as it desires. The relationship is voluntary, based on mutual love and confidence, and is in no sense maintained by force or coercion. A church may withdraw at any time for reasons that seem sufficient to it, provided the congregation is given at least thirty days notice of the meeting at which the withdrawal is to be voted.

If a church is dissolved by presbytery at the congregation’s request and no disposition of its property has been made within six months, those who held title deliver and convey it to the presbytery, which applies the property or its proceeds at its discretion.

s.h: The contrast that makes the point

b.p: In the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) all property held by or for a congregation is held in trust for that denomination, and the relationship of a congregation to the denomination may be severed only by constitutional action on the part of the presbytery. The PCA’s book takes the opposite path on both points.

b.n: This is one of the sharpest practical differences between American Presbyterian bodies, and it explains much of the property litigation of the last century. It also explains why the PCA’s founding congregations could leave with their buildings.

qz.q: Under BCO 25-9, a congregation’s property is
o: held in trust for the presbytery
held in trust for the General Assembly
owned by the congregation, with no right of reversion to any court
owned jointly by the church and the presbytery
qz.w: Chapter 25 is also framed as a solemn covenant that the church will never try to take a congregation’s property against its will.

qz.q: How much notice must a congregation have before voting to withdraw from the PCA?
qz.w: The relationship is voluntary and may be ended for reasons that seem sufficient to the congregation.

qz.q: In the PC(USA), a congregation’s relationship to the denomination can be severed
o: only by constitutional action of the presbytery
qz.w: Its property is held in trust for the denomination under G-4.0203.

lessons.d: How a mission church is begun, governed for a time, and constituted as a particular church.

b.p: Mission churches are ordinarily established by presbyteries within their bounds. A presbytery may act on its own initiative, respond to the initiative of a Session, or answer the written petition of an independent gathering of believers who wish to become a congregation. Where an existing non-PCA church wishes to come in, presbytery works with its leadership to decide whether it should enter as a mission church or seek reception under 13-8.

If a mission church lies outside the bounds of a presbytery, responsibility may be exercised through the Assembly’s committee on Mission to North America or Mission to the World, which then exercises the powers given to presbytery in these provisions. Should it become necessary, presbytery may dissolve a mission church, caring for its members by the procedures used when a church is dissolved.

Because of its transitional condition, a mission church needs a temporary system of government. At its discretion presbytery may appoint an evangelist, may cooperate with the Session of a particular church in a mother and daughter relationship so that the Session serves as the temporary governing body, or may appoint a commission to serve as a temporary Session, in which case a minister approved to serve as pastor is included and serves as moderator. The temporary government records its acts and submits its records to presbytery for annual review like any Session.

Pastoral ministry may be provided by a minister called by presbytery to serve as pastor, by stated, student or ruling elder supply, or by a series of qualified preachers approved by the temporary government. The temporary government receives members under the provisions of chapter 57 so far as they apply, and those received are communing or non-communing members of the Presbyterian Church in America. Mission churches have the right of judicial process to the court overseeing their temporary government.

A new church can be organised only by the authority of presbytery. A presbytery should have standing rules setting the prerequisites that qualify a mission church to begin the process, such as the minimum number of petitioners and the level of financial support, and the number of officers sufficient for a Session quorum is necessary to complete it.

l: The temporary government oversees the steps and, when men appear qualified, begins the nomination and election process under chapter 24 so far as it applies.
Elections normally take place at least two weeks before the organization service, though the new officers take office at the completion of that service.
If no deacons are elected, their duties fall to the Session until deacons can be secured.

Where a minister approved to serve as pastor is in place and members have been received, the temporary Session may call a congregational meeting at which the congregation may call him as pastor by majority vote without the steps of chapter 20. Otherwise a pastor is called under chapter 20 so far as it applies.
The members sign a petition to presbytery asking to be organised, and on approval presbytery appoints an organizing commission and sets the date and time of the service.

b.p: At the service the commission ordains and installs the officers, ordains or installs a pastor where that is part of the service, asks the communicant members present to enter into covenant by answering a question with uplifted hand, promising to walk together as a particular church on the principles of the faith and order of this church and to be zealous and faithful in maintaining the purity and peace of the whole body, and then declares them constituted a church according to the Word of God.

Once organised, the new Session should meet as soon as practicable to elect a stated clerk and form a budget. If there is no pastor, the Session may elect a moderator from its own number or any teaching elder of presbytery with presbytery’s approval, and must act to secure the regular administration of Word and Sacraments.

qz.q: A mission church is governed
o: by a temporary system of government provided by presbytery
qz.w: The options are an evangelist, a mother church Session, or a commission serving as a temporary Session.

qz.q: A new church can be organised
o: by the members petitioning a Session
only by the authority of presbytery
by the Assembly's committee in all cases
qz.w: Presbytery approves the petition, appoints an organizing commission and sets the service.

qz.q: If deacons are not elected when a church is organised,
o: their duties fall to the Session until deacons can be secured
qz.w: The same rule appears in chapter 9 for any church that cannot secure deacons.

lessons.d: Two senses of the word, three ends, and the order the steps must follow.

b.p: Discipline is the exercise of authority given the church by the Lord Jesus Christ to instruct and guide its members and to promote its purity and welfare. The term has two senses: the whole government, inspection, training, guardianship and control the church maintains over its members, officers and courts; and a restricted, technical sense meaning judicial process.
All baptized persons, being members of the church, are subject to its discipline and entitled to its benefits.

Discipline maintains the glory of God, the purity of his church, and the keeping and reclaiming of disobedient sinners. So far as it involves judicial action, its ends are the rebuke of offenses, the removal of scandal, the vindication of the honour of Christ, the promotion of the purity and general edification of the church, and the spiritual good of offenders themselves.

The power Christ has given the church is for building up and not for destruction, and is exercised under a dispensation of mercy rather than of wrath. As in preaching the wicked are doctrinally separated from the good, so by discipline the church authoritatively separates between the holy and the profane, acting the part of a tender mother correcting her children for their good.

b.q: Church censures are necessary, for the reclaiming and gaining of offending brethren, for deterring of others from the like offenses, for purging out of that leaven which might infect the whole lump, for vindicating the honor of Christ, and the holy profession of the gospel, and for preventing the wrath of God.

b.p: Scriptural law is the basis of all discipline because it is the revelation of God’s holy will. The proper principles are instruction in the Word; the responsibility of individuals to admonish one another; if admonition is rejected, the calling of one or more witnesses; and if rejection persists, action by the church through her court unto admonition, suspension, excommunication and deposition. These steps must be followed in proper order.

Teaching elders are charged to instruct the officers in discipline, to instruct the congregation in discipline, and to practise it jointly in the context of the congregation and the church courts. Discipline that is unknown until it is used will always look arbitrary.

The spiritual nurture, instruction and training of the children of the church are committed by God primarily to their parents, who are responsible to the church for the discharge of their obligations. The church should maintain constant and sympathetic relations with the children, encourage them, when they come to years of discretion, to confess Christ and seek admission to the Lord’s Supper, and where they are wayward should cherish them and use every means to reclaim them.

qz.q: The two senses of discipline in BCO 27-1 are
o: the whole government and training of the church, and judicial process
qz.w: Most of what a Session does day by day is discipline in the first sense.

qz.q: Which is not named among the ends of judicial discipline?
o: The vindication of the honour of Christ
The punishment of the offender for its own sake
The spiritual good of offenders themselves
qz.w: The power is given for building up, not for destruction.

qz.q: BCO 27-5 requires that the scriptural steps
o: be used at the court's discretion
qz.w: The steps run from instruction, through private admonition and witnesses, to the action of the court.

lessons.d: What may be charged, and the five censures a court may impose.

b.p: An offense, the proper object of judicial process, is anything in the doctrines or practice of a church member professing faith in Christ that is contrary to the Word of God. The Confession and Catechisms, with the formularies of government, discipline and worship, are accepted as standard expositions of the teachings of Scripture in relation to faith and practice. Nothing may be considered an offense, or admitted as a matter of accusation, which cannot be proved to be such from Scripture as interpreted in these standards.

Offenses are personal or general, private or public, and all of them, being sins against God, are grounds of discipline. Personal offenses are violations of divine law considered as wrongs or injuries to particular individuals; general offenses are heresies or immoralities having no such relation, or considered apart from it. Private offenses are known only to a few; public offenses are notorious.

b.n: Personal and private are not synonyms, and the pair of distinctions matters in practice. Whether an offense is personal decides whether the Matthew 18 steps must come first. Whether it is public shapes how the censure is administered.

l: Admonition: the formal reproof of an offender by a court, warning him of his guilt and danger and exhorting him to be more circumspect and watchful.
Suspension from the Sacraments: temporary exclusion from them, always indefinite as to duration. There is no definite suspension from the Sacraments.
Suspension from office: the exclusion of an officer from his office, which may be definite or indefinite.
Excommunication: the excision of an offender from the communion of the church, inflicted only for gross crime or heresy where the offender shows himself incorrigible and contumacious.
Deposition: the degradation of an officer from his office, which may or may not be accompanied by other censure.

b.p: Admonition or definite suspension from office is administered to a convicted person who satisfies the court as to his repentance and makes appropriate restitution, and such a censure concludes the judicial process. Indefinite suspension or excommunication is administered to one who, upon conviction, remains impenitent.

For officers, suspension from the Sacraments always carries suspension from office with it, though suspension from office does not always carry suspension from the Sacraments. Definite suspension from office is used where the credit of religion, the honour of Christ and the good of the delinquent require it, even though he has satisfied the court.

Censures and the modes of administering them are suited to the nature of the offense. For private offenses, censure is administered in the presence of the court alone, or privately by one or more of its members. For public offenses, the degree and the mode lie within the court’s discretion, following the paragraphs that deal with particular censures.

The book supplies the words for each sentence, to be spoken by the moderator: for definite suspension from office, for indefinite suspension, for excommunication and for deposition. The forms for definite and indefinite suspension were revised in 2026.

qz.q: Which censure is never definite in duration?
qz.w: The book says plainly that there is no definite suspension from the Sacraments.

qz.q: Excommunication is reserved for
o: gross crime or heresy where the offender is incorrigible and contumacious
qz.w: Its design is to reclaim the offender, to deliver the church from scandal, and to inspire fear by the example.

qz.q: An offense may be charged only if it
o: offends a majority of the Session
can be proved contrary to the Word of God as interpreted in the standards
qz.w: BCO 29-1 closes the door on charges that rest on preference rather than Scripture.

lessons.d: Who prosecutes, what must be in writing, and the order a trial follows.

b.p: It is the duty of Sessions and presbyteries to exercise care over those under their authority, and with due diligence and great discretion to require satisfactory explanations concerning reports affecting a person’s Christian character. That duty is more imperative where a person who believes himself wronged by injurious reports asks for an investigation. If the investigation raises a strong presumption of guilt, the court institutes process and appoints a prosecutor to prepare the indictment and conduct the case.

The original and only parties in a case of process are the accuser and the accused, and the accuser is always the Presbyterian Church in America, whose honour and purity are to be maintained. The prosecutor, voluntary or appointed, always represents the church. Every indictment begins in the name of this church and concludes against the peace, unity and purity of the church and the honour and majesty of the Lord Jesus Christ as its King and Head.

An injured party may not become the prosecutor of a personal offense without first trying the means of reconciliation and of reclaiming the offender that Christ requires. A court may still investigate a personal offense as if it were general where the interest of religion seems to demand it. Great caution is to be used in receiving accusations from a person known to indulge a malignant spirit, of poor character, himself under censure, deeply interested in a conviction, or known to be litigious, rash or highly imprudent. A voluntary prosecutor is warned beforehand that if he fails to show probable cause he may himself be censured as a slanderer of the brethren.

When a member of a court is under process, all his official functions may be administratively suspended at the court’s discretion. This is never done by way of censure, and it requires a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, abstentions not counted, at the meeting of the Session or presbytery, even where a commission is conducting the process. That requirement was amended in 2026. In discussion of questions in his own case, the accused has the rights of a defendant only, not of a judge.

Process is not commenced unless some person undertakes to make out the charge, or the court finds it necessary for the honour of religion to act itself. When a charge is laid before a Session or presbytery it is reduced to writing, and nothing is done at the first meeting, except by consent of parties, but three things: appointing a prosecutor; ordering the indictment drawn and a copy served on the accused with the names of known witnesses; and citing the accused to appear at another meeting not sooner than ten days later.

At that second meeting the charges are read to the accused and he is called on to plead. If he confesses, the court may deal with him at its discretion. If he pleads and takes issue, the trial is scheduled and the parties and witnesses cited, and the trial is not sooner than fourteen days after that citation. In drawing the indictment the times, places and circumstances should be stated particularly, so that the accused can make his defense.

An accused who refuses to obey a citation is cited a second time with notice that he will be dealt with for contumacy if he does not appear. One who appears and refuses to plead, or otherwise refuses to cooperate with lawful proceedings, is likewise dealt with for contumacy.
It is appropriate that with each citation the moderator or clerk draw the parties’ attention to the Rules of Discipline and help them obtain access to them.

When the trial is about to begin, the moderator announces from the chair that the court is passing to the consideration of the case, and charges the members to remember their character as judges of a court of Jesus Christ. Witnesses are examined in the presence of the accused, or at least after due citation, and may be cross-examined by both parties.

l: The moderator charges the court.
The indictment is read and the answer of the accused is heard.
The witnesses for the prosecutor are examined, then those for the accused.
The parties are heard, first the prosecutor, then the accused, and the prosecutor closes.
The roll is called and members may express their opinion.
The vote is taken, the verdict announced, and judgment entered on the records.

b.p: Either party may challenge for cause the right of any member to sit, and the other members decide. A member who expresses his opinion of the merits to a party or to anyone outside the court, or who absents himself from a sitting without permission or satisfactory reason, is disqualified from taking further part.

The clerk keeps minutes exhibiting the charges, the answer, the record of testimony, the orders and decisions either party desires, and the judgment. He assembles without delay the Record of the Case, which consists of the charges, the answer, the citations and returns, and the required minutes. Parties may have copies at their own expense. Where a case is removed by appeal or complaint, the lower court sends up that Record with the notice and reasons, and nothing outside the Record is taken into consideration by the higher court.

No professional counsel may appear and plead as such in any court. An accused person may be represented before a Session or presbytery by any member in good standing of a church in the same presbytery, or by any teaching elder member of that presbytery, and before the General Assembly by any member in good standing in this church. A member of the court so employed may not sit in judgment in the case. Courts are encouraged to suggest names of potential representatives and advisors. This section was widened in 2025.

The accused or a member of the court may object to consideration of a charge, for example where the passage of time since the alleged offense makes fair adjudication unachievable. The court weighs factors such as the gravity of the alleged offense and the degradation of evidence and memory in the intervening period.

qz.q: At the first meeting after a charge is laid, the court may, without consent of parties,
o: appoint a prosecutor, order the indictment drawn and served, and cite the accused
qz.w: The citation must give at least ten days before the next meeting.

qz.q: Who is always the accuser in a case of process?
qz.w: The prosecutor is the church’s representative and has all its rights in the case.

qz.q: May an attorney represent an accused person as professional counsel?
o: No, though the accused may be represented by a qualified member of this church
qz.w: A member of the court who serves as representative may not sit in judgment in the case.

qz.q: The administrative suspension of a court member under process requires
o: a majority of the commission trying the case
two-thirds of the members present and voting at the Session or presbytery
qz.w: It is never done by way of censure, and the 2026 amendment made clear that the two-thirds vote belongs to the court even where a commission conducts the process.

lessons.d: The special rules for Sessions and for ministers, and the law of proof.

b.p: Process against all church members other than ministers is entered before the Session of the church to which they belong, except in cases of appeal. If a Session refuses to act in doctrinal cases or instances of public scandal, and two other Sessions of churches in the same presbytery ask the presbytery to initiate appropriate action and assume jurisdiction, the presbytery must do so.

A member found contumacious is immediately suspended from the Sacraments, and from office if he holds one, for his contumacy. The fact and the charges are recorded, and the censure may be made public if the Session deems it expedient. It is not removed until he has repented of the contumacy and given satisfaction on the charges. If he persists after further endeavour, he is excommunicated.

Where it is impracticable to commence process at once, the Session may, if it judges that the church’s edification requires it, keep the accused from the Lord’s Table until the charges can be examined. That requires a two-thirds majority.

Process against a minister is entered before the presbytery of which he is a member. If a presbytery refuses to act in doctrinal cases or cases of public scandal and two other presbyteries ask the General Assembly to assume original jurisdiction, the Assembly must do so.

As no minister ought to be screened in his sin or slightly censured on account of his office, so scandalous charges ought not to be received against him on slight grounds. One who knows a minister to be guilty of a private offense should warn him privately; if the offense is persisted in or becomes public, he should bring it to the attention of another minister of the presbytery.

A minister found contumacious is immediately suspended from the Sacraments and his office, and that censure is made public. If he persists, he is deposed and excommunicated. Where a minister confesses during trial to a matter that is base and flagitious, the court, however penitent he appears, without delay imposes definite suspension or deposes him.

A minister under indefinite suspension or deposed for scandalous conduct is not restored, even on the deepest sorrow for sin, until he has shown for a considerable time a life and testimony that heal the wound made by his scandal. A deposed minister is restored only where the general sentiment of the church is strongly in his favour, and then only by the court that imposed the censure or with its consent, by a three-fourths vote.

Where a minister habitually fails to discharge his official functions, presbytery inquires into the cause at a stated meeting and may institute judicial proceedings for breach of his covenant engagement. If the neglect proceeds only from his lack of acceptance in the church, presbytery may divest him of office without censure, even against his will, by a two-thirds majority, after written notice stating the grounds and a hearing in his own defense, and he may appeal as if tried in the usual form. The principle may be applied to ruling elders and deacons with the necessary changes.

All persons of proper age and intelligence are competent witnesses, except those who do not believe in the existence of God or in a future state of rewards and punishments, and either party may challenge a witness as incompetent, with the court deciding. The accused is allowed but not compelled to testify; the accuser must testify on the accused’s demand; and a husband or wife is not compelled to testify against the other.

A court may make reasonable accommodation to prevent in-person contact with the accused, including testimony by videoconference in which all can see and hear one another and live cross-examination is possible, restriction of the accused from appearing on screen with cross-examination conducted by his representative, and written interrogatories read to witnesses under eighteen. Its reasons and any objection are recorded.

The testimony of more than one witness is necessary to establish a charge, though corroborative evidence added to one witness may prove the offense. The court judges the degree of credibility due to all evidence. Witnesses are examined first by the party introducing them, then cross-examined, and afterwards questioned by the court, and no frivolous or irrelevant question is permitted. The oath is administered by the moderator in the form the book supplies, with liberty for a witness who prefers another manner of swearing or affirming.

All parts of a trial other than deliberations are recorded, by transcription, audio, video or other electronic means, and the witnesses are told so before testifying. The recording becomes part of the Record of the Case, and must be transcribed and authenticated by the trial court before it can be cited in briefs. That provision was amended in 2026. If new testimony is discovered after trial, the accused may ask for a new trial and the court has power to grant it.

lessons.t: Censure, Restoration and Cases Without Process
lessons.d: Lifting a censure, raising one, and judging on confession without a trial.

b.p: A person definitely suspended from office is restored by the court at the end of his term with words the book supplies. After indefinite suspension from the Sacraments, the rulers of the church should converse with him frequently and pray with him and for him. When the court is satisfied as to the reality of his repentance, he professes it before the court or publicly, and is restored to the Sacraments, and to his office if the court so judges.

An excommunicated person brought to repentance answers three questions confessing his sin and rebellion, professing repentance, and promising to live circumspectly, and the minister pronounces the sentence of restoration. A deposed officer is restored after public confession in similar form, and a ruling elder or deacon so absolved cannot resume the exercise of his office without re-election by the people. Removing a sentence of deposition takes a three-fourths vote of the court that imposed it.

Where a person under censure lives too far from the court that sentenced him for oversight to be practical, the court may, with his acquiescence and the concurrence of the receiving court, transmit a certified copy of its proceedings to the court where he lives, which assumes jurisdiction. In restoring a minister, presbytery proceeds with great caution: first admitting him to the Sacraments if he was debarred, then granting him the privilege of preaching on probation to test the sincerity of his repentance and the prospect of his usefulness, and the case remains under judicial consideration until restoration is declared.

Where members of a court wish to consider raising an indefinite suspension, from office or from the Sacraments, to deposition or excommunication, they need not begin process afresh. The indefinitely suspended person is not in good standing and has already been found impenitent. He has, however, a right to a hearing. The court may consider a motion to find him incorrigible and contumacious and present evidence to that effect, must give him at least thirty days notice of such a motion, and must permit him the privilege of the floor to plead and give evidence of repentance before the court having jurisdiction, and not before a trial commission. After the hearing the court votes on whether to raise the censure, and a person whose suspension is so raised has the right of appeal. This whole section was added in 2026, and the list of those entitled to appeal was amended to match.

Where a person comes forward and makes his offense known to the court, a full statement of the facts is recorded and judgment is rendered without process. The person must intend to confess and to let the court render judgment without process. Statements made in the court’s presence are not taken as the basis of judgment without his consent. A written confession, containing a sufficient summary of the facts, his specific confession, and any expression or evidence of repentance, must be approved by the accused and by the court before judgment, and the co-signed document is appended to the minutes. No other information may be presented without the written consent of the accused and the court.

Where a personal offense is involved, the court must try to inform the offended person of the part of the confession it deems pertinent, invite comment on it before final approval, encourage that person to enlist an advisor, and report how the offended were informed. A censured person keeps the right of appeal and the right to be assisted by a representative.

A minister against whom there are no charges, who is fully satisfied in his own conscience that God has not called him to the ministry, or who has satisfactory evidence of his inability to serve the church with acceptance, may report the facts at a stated meeting. At the next stated meeting, if presbytery concurs after full deliberation, it may divest him of office without censure. The same provision applies, with the necessary changes, to ruling elders and deacons, with the Session acting as presbytery acts.

lessons.t: How Higher Courts Review Lower Courts
lessons.d: Four modes of supervision, the annual reading of records, and the four standards of review.

b.p: The acts and decisions of a lower court come under the supervision of a higher court in one of four ways: review and control, reference, appeal and complaint. When the proceedings of a lower court are before a higher court, the members of the lower court keep their right to sit, deliberate and vote, except in cases of appeal or complaint.

It is the right and duty of every court above the Session to review, at least once a year, the records of the court next below. If a lower court fails to present its records, the higher court may require them immediately or at a time it fixes.

l: Whether the proceedings have been correctly recorded.
Whether they have been regular and in accordance with the Constitution.
Whether they have been wise, equitable and suited to promote the welfare of the church.
Whether the lawful injunctions of the higher court have been obeyed.

b.p: Ordinarily the higher court simply records whether it approves, disapproves or corrects the records in any particular. Where a serious irregularity appears, it may require review and correction by the lower court. Proceedings in judicial cases are not dealt with under review and control once notice of appeal or complaint has been given, and no judgment in a judicial case is reversed except by appeal or complaint.

Courts sometimes neglect their duty altogether, so that heretical opinions or corrupt practices gain ground, gross offenders escape, or irregular proceedings go unrecorded. Where the next higher court is well advised of such neglect or irregularity, it must take cognizance of the matter and examine, deliberate and judge as completely as if it had come up by review of records.

Where a court with appellate jurisdiction receives a credible report of important delinquency or grossly unconstitutional proceedings in the court below, the first step is to cite that court to appear, by representative or in writing, at a specified time and place, and to show what it has done or failed to do. The citing court may then reverse or redress the proceedings in other than judicial cases, censure the delinquent court, remit the matter with an injunction to dispose of it constitutionally, or stay further proceedings.

The Constitution is fallible and subordinate to Scripture, and it has been adopted by the church as a standard exposition of Scripture’s teaching. To keep it from being amended, violated or disregarded in judicial process, any review of the judicial proceedings of a lower court is guided by four principles.

l: The higher court limits itself to the issues raised by the parties in the original court, and resolves them by applying the Constitution as established through the constitutional process.

It ordinarily shows great deference to the lower court on factual matters the lower court is more competent to determine, because of its proximity to events and its personal knowledge of the parties and witnesses, and does not reverse a factual finding unless there is clear error.

It shows the same deference on matters of discretion and judgment that only a court with familiar acquaintance of the events and parties can address, such as the moral character of candidates for office, the appropriate censure after a trial, or the comparative credibility of conflicting witnesses, and does not reverse unless there is clear error.

It owes no such deference on the interpretation of the Constitution, where it has the duty and authority to interpret and apply according to its best ability and understanding, whatever the lower court's opinion.

b.n: Read together, these four sentences explain most outcomes on appeal. A party who wants a factual finding reversed must show clear error. A party arguing that the lower court misread the Constitution is not asking for deference at all.

lessons.d: Three named routes upward, and how to tell which one a case needs.

b.p: A reference is a written representation and application made by a lower court to a higher one for advice or other action on a matter still pending below, ordinarily to the next higher court. Proper subjects are matters that are new, delicate or difficult, or on which the members are seriously divided, or which involve the Constitution and legal procedures where the lower court feels the need of guidance.

A lower court may ask for advice only, or for final disposition. In particular it may refer a judicial case with a request that the higher court take original jurisdiction of the case, its trial, judgment and whatever censure it deems warranted; or that the higher court provide additional teaching and ruling elders to serve with the lower court in the case, who during their service have all the rights and responsibilities of judges there, subject to the parties’ right of challenge. That provision was amended in 2026.

Although references are sometimes proper, in general it is better that every court discharge the duty assigned it under the law of the church. A higher court is not required to accede, but should ordinarily give advice when it is requested.

An appeal is the transfer to a higher court of a judicial case on which judgment has been rendered below, and is allowable only to the party against whom the decision was rendered. It cannot be taken to any court other than the next higher, except with that court’s consent.

Those entitled to appeal are those who have submitted to a regular trial, those appealing a censure in a case without process, those appealing the raising of a censure under 36-8, and those appealing a divestiture without censure under 34-10.

The grounds are such as these: irregularity in the proceedings of the lower court; refusal of reasonable indulgence to a party on trial; receiving improper evidence or declining to receive proper evidence; hurrying to a decision before all the testimony is taken; manifestation of prejudice in the case; and mistake or injustice in the judgment and censure.

Notice of appeal may be given before the court adjourns, and written notice with supporting reasons must be filed with the clerk of the lower court and the clerk of the higher court within thirty days of notification of the decision. The clerk of the lower court files the Record of the Case with the higher court within thirty days of receiving notice. Notice of appeal suspends the judgment until the case is decided, though the court of original jurisdiction may, for recorded reasons, keep the appellant from the Lord’s Table or from some or all official functions, never as censure and only by a two-thirds majority.

At the hearing, after the Record is read, each side has not over thirty minutes for oral argument, the appellant opening and closing. The court or commission then goes into closed session and votes on each specification of error in the form: shall this specification of error be sustained. The decision may affirm in whole or part, reverse in whole or part, render the decision that should have been rendered, or remand for a new trial, and a written opinion is always prepared. An appellant who fails to appear is considered to have abandoned his appeal, and one who manifests a litigious or otherwise unchristian spirit receives a suitable rebuke.

A complaint is a written representation made against some act or decision of a court. Any communing member of the church in good standing may complain against any action of a court to whose jurisdiction he is subject, except that no complaint is allowable in a judicial case after process has commenced. Where such a complaint is timely filed after process has begun, its adjudication waits until the judicial case is complete or any appeal is finished or withdrawn. That provision was amended in 2025.

A complaint is made first to the court whose act is alleged to be in error, with written notice and supporting reasons filed with its clerk within sixty days following the meeting. The court considers it at its next stated meeting, or at a called meeting before then, provided the complaint was filed at least ten days in advance. If the court denies the complaint, or fails to consider it, the complainant may take it to the next higher court by filing written notice with both clerks within thirty days of notification.

Notice of complaint does not suspend the action complained against unless a third of the members present when the action was taken vote for suspension until the higher court decides. The court complained against appoints one or more representatives to defend its action, and the parties are known as complainant and respondent. The complainant may present his own complaint or may have the help of a communing member of this church in good standing.

The higher court may annul the whole or any part of the action complained against, or send the matter back with instructions for a new hearing. Where it rules that a lower court erred by not indicting someone, and the lower court refers the matter back, it must accept the reference in a doctrinal case or a case of public scandal.

An appeal belongs to a party against whom a judgment was rendered in a judicial case. A complaint belongs to any communing member who thinks a court acted wrongly, and is not available inside a judicial case once process has begun. A reference comes from the court itself, before it has decided. Review and control needs no one to file anything, because the records go up every year.

lessons.t: Principles of Worship and the Lord’s Day
lessons.d: What the Directory is, what it binds, and the elements it names.

s.h: What kind of document this is

b.p: A statement adopted by the third General Assembly prefaces the Directory: it is an approved guide, to be taken seriously as the mind of the church agreeable to the standards, which does not have the force of law and is not obligatory in all its parts. Chapters 56, 57 and 58 were later given full constitutional authority after two-thirds of the presbyteries approved, and section 59-3 was given the same authority in the same way.

Since the Holy Scriptures are the only infallible rule of faith and practice, the principles of public worship must be derived from the Bible and from no other source. Scripture forbids worshipping God by images or in any way not appointed in his Word, and requires the receiving, observing and keeping pure and entire all such religious worship and ordinances as God has appointed.

b.q: The acceptable way of worshiping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshiped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture.

b.p: A service of public worship is not merely a gathering of God’s children with each other, but before all else a meeting of the triune God with his chosen people. Its end is the glory of God, and its aim the building of Christ’s church. The Lord Jesus has prescribed no fixed forms, and in the interest of life and power in worship has given his church a large measure of liberty, within the rules of his Word, so that all things are done decently and in order.

The proper elements of a worship service are the reading of Holy Scripture, the singing of psalms and hymns, the offering of prayer, the preaching of the Word, the presentation of offerings, confessing the faith, and observing the Sacraments, with oaths on special occasions.

God commanded his Old Testament people to keep the last day of the week holy, and sanctified the first day as the Sabbath by the resurrection of Christ, so that the church of the new dispensation has kept the first day holy since the time of the apostles. The whole day is to be kept holy and employed in the public and private exercises of religion, with a holy resting from unnecessary labours and from recreations lawful on other days.

Households are to order the day so that no one is improperly detained from public worship, and the time not spent in public worship is given to prayer, devotional reading and the study of Scripture, meditation, catechizing, religious conversation, singing, visiting the sick, relieving the poor, teaching the ignorant and holy resting.

l: Reading of Scripture: performed by the minister as God's servant, through which God speaks most directly to the congregation, read from a good translation and not a paraphrase.

Singing: praise in song is a duty and a privilege, psalms are recommended alongside hymns with care in selection, the leadership in song is left to the Session's judgment, and a choir is not to displace congregational singing.

Prayer: a full and comprehensive prayer before the sermon, with adoration, thanksgiving, confession, supplication, pleading and intercession, offered in the language of the people; ministers are not confined to fixed forms but are to prepare for this part of their work.

Preaching: the text should fairly contain the doctrine handled and not serve as a motto; sermons require study, meditation and prayer, and should keep to the simplicity of the gospel; no one preaches in our churches without the consent of the Session.
Offerings: God owns all and we are stewards, and the acknowledgment takes the form in part of giving at least a tithe, in regular, weekly, systematic and proportionate offerings.
Confessing the faith: it is proper to confess the faith publicly using creeds true to the Word, such as the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed or the Westminster Standards.

lessons.t: Baptism, Profession and the Lord’s Supper
lessons.d: The three chapters of the Directory that carry the force of law.

b.p: Baptism is not to be unnecessarily delayed, and is not administered by any private person but by a minister of Christ. It is not administered privately, but in the presence of the congregation and under the supervision of the Session. The child is presented by one or both parents, or some other responsible person.

Before baptism the minister instructs the people about the institution, nature, use and ends of the sacrament: that Christ instituted it; that it is a seal of the covenant of grace, of ingrafting into Christ and union with him, of remission of sins, regeneration, adoption and eternal life; that the water signifies both the blood of Christ and the sanctifying power of his Spirit; that the promise is made to believers and their children; that children are solemnly received into the bosom of the visible church; that the inward grace is not tied to the moment of administration; and that covenant children, on reaching the age of discretion, become subject to the obligations of the covenant and must make public confession or become covenant breakers subject to the discipline of the church.

Parents are exhorted to teach the child to read the Word of God, to instruct him in the principles of the Christian religion as summarised in the Confession and Catechisms, to pray with and for him, and to set an example of piety and godliness. The minister reads the covenant promises, puts three questions to the parents, and may put an optional question to the congregation about assisting the parents in the child’s Christian nurture. He then baptizes the child, by pouring or sprinkling water on the head, without adding any other ceremony.

Believers’ children within the visible church, and especially those dedicated to God in baptism, are non-communing members under the care of the church. When they are able to understand the gospel they should be earnestly reminded that they are members of the church by birthright, and that it is their duty and privilege to accept Christ personally, confess him before men, and seek admission to the Lord’s Supper. The Session judges, after careful examination, the qualifications of those who apply.

The five membership vows follow, and those received from other churches by letter, or by reaffirmation, give a testimony of their Christian experience to the Session and are announced to the congregation.

The Communion is to be observed frequently, at times the Session of each congregation determines as most for edification. The ignorant and the scandalous are not to be admitted. Public notice should be given at least the Sabbath before, and the people instructed in the nature of the ordinance and in due preparation for it.

On the day of observance, after the sermon, the minister shows that this is an ordinance of Christ, reading the words of institution, and that it is observed in remembrance of him. Since the sacrament sets forth the communion of saints, the minister, at the discretion of the Session, may either invite all those who profess the true religion and are communicants in good standing in any evangelical church, or invite those whom the Session has approved after they have indicated their desire to participate. It is proper also to give a special invitation to non-communicants to remain during the service.

The elements are set apart by prayer and thanksgiving, the bread is broken in view of the people and distributed with the words of institution, and the cup likewise. Part of the time of distribution is properly spent in silent communion, thanksgiving, intercession and prayer. An offering for the poor or another sacred purpose is appropriate, and congregations are urged to hold a service of spiritual preparation in the week before.

b.n: The two forms of invitation in 58-4 are both constitutional, and the choice between them belongs to the Session. Practice differs widely from congregation to congregation for that reason, not because some churches are ignoring the book.

lessons.t: Marriage, the Sick, Burial and the Home
lessons.d: The remaining chapters of the Directory, and the one section among them that is law.

b.p: Marriage is a divine institution, though not a sacrament and not peculiar to the church of Christ. It is proper that every commonwealth should make laws to regulate marriage, which citizens are bound to obey so far as those laws do not transgress the laws of God. Christians should marry in the Lord, and it is fit that their marriage be solemnized by a lawful minister, with special instruction and suitable prayers.

Marriage is only to be between one man and one woman, in accordance with the Word of God, and ministers in this church who solemnize marriages shall only solemnize marriages between one man and one woman. This section carries full constitutional authority.

The parties should be of years of discretion, able to make their own choice, and where they are under age or live with parents the consent of those under whose care they are should be obtained and certified to the minister. Parents should neither compel their children to marry against their inclinations nor withhold consent without just and important reasons. Because marriage is of a public nature, its purpose should be sufficiently published beforehand, and ministers are to obey the laws of the community so far as those laws do not transgress the laws of God as the Constitution of this church interprets them. The minister keeps a proper register of the marriages he performs.

The power of the prayer of faith is great, and Christians should make entreaty for the sick and seek God’s blessing on the means employed for recovery. When a person is sick, the minister or an officer of the church should be told, so that minister, officers and members may unite in prayer. It is the privilege and duty of the pastor to visit the sick and to minister to their physical, mental and spiritual welfare, using discretion in varying circumstances.

The services proper at a burial are the singing of appropriate psalms or hymns, the reading of suitable portions of Scripture with such remarks as seem proper to the minister, and prayer in which the bereaved are especially remembered. The service is left largely to the minister’s discretion, but its proper object is the worship of God and the consolation of the living.

Observing days of fasting and thanksgiving as providence directs is both scriptural and rational. They may be observed by individuals, families, particular congregations, groups of congregations, the congregations of a presbytery, or all the congregations of the church. Individuals and families judge for themselves, Sessions judge for congregations, presbyteries for larger districts, and where a fast or thanksgiving should be general the call is issued by the General Assembly.

Besides public worship, it is the duty of each person in secret and of every family in private to worship God. Secret worship is plainly enjoined by our Lord, and includes prayer, reading the Scriptures, holy meditation and serious self-examination. Family worship, which every family should observe, consists in prayer, reading the Scriptures and singing praises, or some briefer form of outspoken recognition of God. Parents instruct their children in the Word and in the principles of religion, set an example of piety and consistent living, and cooperate with the church in the children’s religious education.

lessons.d: Three steps for the book, three-fourths at every step for the Standards, and where an idea starts.

s.h: Amending the Book of Church Order

l: Approval of the proposed amendment by a majority of those present and voting in the General Assembly, and its recommendation to the presbyteries.
The advice and consent of two-thirds of the presbyteries.
Approval and enactment by a subsequent General Assembly, by a majority of those present and voting.

b.p: In voting on an amendment, presbyteries may not divide its parts except as the Assembly that recommended it directs. Where enough presbyteries fail to act or to report that the response is unsatisfactory, the next Assembly may defer action for a year and urge the delinquent presbyteries to report.

The doctrinal standards are harder to move. Amendment requires three-fourths of those present and voting in the Assembly, then the advice and consent of three-fourths of the presbyteries, then approval and enactment by a subsequent Assembly by three-fourths of those present and voting. The paragraph setting that rule can itself be amended only by the same method.

Full organic union with another ecclesiastical body follows the same three-fourths pattern at each of three steps, and that paragraph is likewise protected. Receiving another body under the Assembly’s jurisdiction, short of organic union, requires the consent of three-fourths of the presbyteries.

An overture is ordinarily the request of a presbytery for action by the General Assembly on a specific matter, and presbytery has power to propose to the Assembly such measures as may be of common advantage to the church at large.

All overtures are published in the commissioner handbook. Overtures requesting amendment of the Book of Church Order or the Assembly’s rules go to the Committee on Constitutional Business for its advice, and overtures proposing amendment of the Constitution go to the Overtures Committee. The stated clerk’s referral is final unless the Assembly redirects it by vote.

b.n: So the practical path of a change runs: an idea, a presbytery that adopts it as an overture, a committee that studies it, an Assembly that sends it down, the presbyteries that vote, and a second Assembly that enacts it. A single Assembly cannot alter the Constitution by itself.

b.p: Sections amended by the 53rd General Assembly: 12-3, 18-2, 24-1, 29-1 as an editorial change, 31-10, 35-9, 36-4, 36-5, 36-8, 41-3 and 42-2, along with rules of Assembly operation 4-21, 4-22.d and 14-11.a.

l: 12-3: in judicial cases, whether or not the church has a pastor, a Session may elect one of its own members to preside as moderator, or invite a minister of its presbytery to do so.
24-1: a Session may render a decision on Christian experience at any point in the process and judge a man ineligible for the election, whether he was previously ordained or not.

31-10: administratively suspending the official functions of a court member under process takes two-thirds of the members present and voting, abstentions not counted, at the Session or presbytery, even where a commission is conducting the process.
35-9: all parts of a trial other than deliberations are to be recorded, and the recording becomes part of the Record of the Case.
36-4 and 36-5: the forms of words for definite and indefinite suspension were revised.

36-8, new: a court may raise an indefinite suspension to deposition or excommunication without beginning process again, after at least thirty days notice and a hearing before the court having jurisdiction rather than a trial commission; 42-2 now lists such a person among those entitled to appeal.
41-3: a reference may ask the higher court to take original jurisdiction of a judicial case, or to provide additional teaching and ruling elders to sit with the lower court as judges.

Assembly rule 4-21, new: committees and commissions established by the book and by those rules may meet electronically if they so determine, except the Overtures Committee and committees of commissioners.

b.n: The 2026 edition marks the changed lines but does not print the former wording, so 18-2 is listed as amended without a visible redline. What the section now requires is taught in the lesson on candidates.

b.p: Sections amended: 13-6, 32-19 and 43-1, with an editorial change to Appendix H and several to the Assembly’s rules. A presbytery that does not accept a minister seeking admission now records that fact with its rationale, if one is adopted, and communicates the rationale to his current presbytery. Those standing trial were given more options for representation. And a complaint may now be filed after judicial process has commenced, to be adjudicated only after the final disposition of the case to which it pertains.

In 2024 the sections amended were 7-3, 8-2, 9-3 and 38-1, with editorial changes elsewhere. As those sections now stand, unordained people are not to be referred to as, or given the titles of, the ordained offices; elders and deacons are to conform to the biblical requirement of chastity and sexual purity in their descriptions of themselves and in their convictions, character and conduct; and a case handled on confession requires a written confession approved by both the accused and the court, with the offended person informed and invited to comment.

In 2023 the sections amended included 8-8, 14-1, 15-1, 15-3, 16-4, 21-4.e, 24-1, 31-10, 33-4, 35-1 to 35-5, 38-1, 42-2, 42-6, 43-2 and 43-3. As they now stand, officers must be above reproach and Christlike in character, affirming the sinfulness of fallen desires, the reality and hope of progressive sanctification, and commitment to Spirit-empowered victory over sinful temptations, inclinations and actions; and examinations of candidates and nominees give specific attention to potential notorious concerns and to the practical struggle against sinful actions and persistent sinful desires.

b.n: The list of amended sections in each year is taken from the table at the front of the current edition, which is reliable. The descriptions here state what those sections now say, which is not the same thing as a redline against the previous text.

b.p: Amendments take effect as soon as the following Assembly votes to approve them, and the Stated Clerk’s office then updates the digital and printed editions. Proposed amendments now before the presbyteries are tracked on the Assembly’s amendment dashboard.

presbytery approval in every Session case
qz.w: The suspension is administrative and is never imposed as a censure.

qz.q: Which section was added in 2026?
qz.w: It allows an indefinite suspension to be raised without new process, with notice, a hearing and a right of appeal.

lessons.d: Three points of comparison that were checked in each body’s own documents.

b.p: This church has three courts: Session, presbytery and General Assembly. There are no synods.

The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) has four councils: the session for the congregation, the presbytery for a district, the synod as an intermediate council for a region, and the General Assembly for the whole church.

s.h: Who sits in the highest court

b.p: In this church the Assembly consists of all teaching elders in good standing, together with ruling elders elected by their Sessions on a fixed formula. It is not a delegated body as to teaching elders.

The Orthodox Presbyterian Church has a delegated assembly of about 150 voting commissioners, ministers and ruling elders commissioned by their presbyteries, with the total fixed by standing rule and the ministerial share capped. In the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) the General Assembly likewise consists of commissioners elected by presbyteries, half ruling elders and half teaching elders.

In this church a congregation owns its property outright, with no right of reversion to any court, and may withdraw at any time for reasons sufficient to it, after at least thirty days notice of the meeting.

In the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) all property held by or for a congregation is held in trust for the denomination, and the relationship of a congregation to the denomination may be severed only by constitutional action of the presbytery.

b.n: This is the difference that most often reaches civil courts, and it is the one to state carefully, because it turns on the text of each body’s constitution rather than on temperament.

b.p: Rules on who may hold office in other denominations were not checked against their own constitutions for this course, so no comparison of that kind is offered here. The same caution applies to any claim about another body’s worship, discipline or doctrine: check that body’s own book before repeating it.

qz.q: Which court exists in the PC(USA) but not in the PCA?
qz.w: The PCA’s courts are Session, presbytery and Assembly.

qz.q: The PCA General Assembly differs from the OPC assembly in that
o: every teaching elder in good standing may sit, rather than a fixed number of commissioners elected by presbyteries
it is a court of first instance
qz.w: The OPC assembly is delegated, with about 150 voting commissioners.

qz.q: A congregation wishing to leave its denomination with its property has the clearest path in
o: the PC(USA), under the trust clause
qz.w: In the PC(USA) the property is held in trust and severance requires presbytery action.

units.d: Where church government comes from, the three answers churches give, and how this one took shape.
A walk through the canon: a people taught and judged, a Shepherd who rules, and churches learning to decide.
The eight principles in front of the book, what the Constitution is, how far church power reaches, and what officers vow.
The visible church, the particular church, and the people on its rolls.
Elders and deacons: calling, qualification, election, ordination.
Session, presbytery and Assembly, and the commissions they appoint.
How a church court actually does business, and what protects the minority in it.
From a man under care to an installed pastor.
Meetings, property, withdrawal, and the planting of churches.
What discipline is for, and how a case is tried.
How a higher court looks at a lower court, and the four ways a matter goes up.
The Directory for Worship, and which parts of it carry the force of law.
How the Constitution is amended, what changed lately, and how other Presbyterian bodies differ.

map.t: The King and Head of the Church
map.s: Christ rules his church from his throne through Word and Spirit by the ministry of men, and has given it officers, oracles and ordinances, with nothing to be added or taken away.

Eight principles on liberty of conscience, a church’s right to set its own terms, discipline, the tie between truth and holiness, forbearance, election of officers, ministerial power and spiritual discipline.
The Constitution is the Westminster Confession and Catechisms together with the Book of Church Order, all subordinate to Scripture.
Five heads of the scriptural, representative form: the church, its members, its officers, its courts, its orders.
One visible church in every age; denominations that keep Word and sacraments in fundamental integrity are true branches.

map.t: The Nature and Extent of Church Power
map.s: Power vests in the whole body, is exercised severally as order and jointly as jurisdiction, is wholly spiritual, and is bounded by the law of Christ.
What a congregation is, who its officers are, where its jurisdiction sits, and what ordinances Christ has given it.

map.t: The Organization of a Particular Church
map.s: Mission churches, the temporary government a presbytery gives them, and the steps by which they are organized as particular churches.
Children of believers are non-communing members; those who profess faith, are baptized and are admitted by the Session are communing members.
Extraordinary offices ceased with the close of revelation; the perpetual classes are elders, in two orders, and deacons, open to men only.
Titles, qualifications and duties of the office, the added functions of teaching elders, evangelists, calls outside the church, chaplains, and the standing of ruling elders.
An office of sympathy and service under the Session, with care of the poor and of church property, and assistants who are not officers.
The courts are Sessions, presbyteries and the General Assembly; all are presbyteries in nature, with moderators, clerks and prayer.
Church courts are distinct from the magistrate, their power is ministerial and declarative, and lower courts are under the review and control of higher ones.
Who sits on a Session, what makes a quorum, who moderates, and the powers by which it governs a congregation.
Its make-up and representation, the membership of ministers, quorum, reception and transfer of ministers, and its powers over churches and officers.
The highest court: its organizing principles, permanent committees, make-up, quorum, powers, and the weight its actions carry.
A commission concludes business, unlike a committee; presbytery commissions, the Standing Judicial Commission and provisional presbyteries abroad.

map.t: Church Orders, The Doctrine of Vocation
map.s: Calling to office is inward testimony, the approval of God’s people and the judgment of a court, and no man is placed over a church without its election or consent.
Officers are inducted by the ordination of a court, with prayer and laying on of hands, and only to a definite work.
Coming under the care of a presbytery: the Session’s endorsement, examination on experiential religion, annual reports, dismissal and removal.
Licensure to preach, the questions put to a licentiate, the four-year term, and an internship of at least a year with its limits.
A call to definite work, the pulpit committee, the congregational election, the form of the call and its prosecution before presbytery.

map.t: The Ordination and Installation of Ministers
map.s: Education, the trials for ordination, examination of character, stated differences with the Standards, the vows, and the service itself.
Pastor, associate pastor and assistant pastor, and the temporary relations of stated, student and ruling elder supply.

map.t: Dissolution of the Pastoral Relation and Honorable Retirement
map.s: How a pastoral relation is dissolved by either party, the limit on an associate or assistant succeeding the pastor, retirement and pastor emeritus.

map.t: Election, Ordination and Installation of Ruling Elders and Deacons
map.s: Nomination, instruction and examination by the Session, the congregational election, the ordination service, and release from active duty.
Who votes, how meetings are called and by what quorum, trustees and corporations, and the property and withdrawal provisions.

map.t: Amending the Constitution of the Church
map.s: Three steps for the Book of Church Order, three-fourths at every step for the Confession and Catechisms, and the terms of organic union.

map.t: Discipline, Its Nature, Subjects and Ends
map.s: Discipline in two senses, its ends, the spirit in which it is used, and the scriptural steps that must be kept in order.
The nurture of covenant children by parents and church, and the care owed to adult non-communing members.
An offense is anything in doctrine or practice contrary to the Word; offenses are personal or general, private or public.
Admonition, suspension from the sacraments, excommunication, suspension from office and deposition, and when each is used.

map.t: The Parties in Cases of Process
map.s: Original jurisdiction, investigation of reports, the Church as accuser, the Matthew 18 requirement, cautions about accusers, and suspension of a court member under process.

map.t: General Provisions Applicable to all Cases of Process
map.s: Charges in writing, citations and their intervals, contumacy, the order of a trial, the Record of the Case, representation, and objection for lapse of time.

map.t: Special Rules Pertaining to Process Before Sessions
map.s: Members are tried by their own Session, with a route to presbytery in doctrinal cases and public scandal, and rules for contumacy and the Table.

map.t: Special Rules Pertaining to Process Against a Minister
map.s: A minister is tried by his presbytery, with a route to the Assembly, care about accusations, confession during trial, restoration, and divestiture without censure.
Competent witnesses, the accused not compelled to testify, accommodations by videoconference, the rule of more than one witness, oaths, and the recording of trials.
The manner of each censure, from private admonition to excommunication and deposition, and the raising of an indefinite suspension.
How censures are lifted and offenders restored, with special caution for ministers, and where jurisdiction sits.
Judgment on a written confession, divestiture at a minister’s own request, attempted withdrawal, and erasure for willful neglect.

map.t: Modes in Which Lower Courts Come Under the Supervision of Higher Courts
map.s: The four modes, the right of lower court members to sit above, and the four standards that govern review of judicial proceedings.
Annual review of records, the four questions reviewers ask, neglected duty, and citation of a lower court on a credible report.
A lower court may ask a higher one for advice or for disposition of a matter, including original jurisdiction or added elders.
Who may appeal, the grounds, the thirty-day notice, the effect on the judgment, the hearing, and the decisions open to the higher court.
Any communing member may complain of an act of a court over him; the filing periods, the effect, the hearing and the powers of the higher court.
This chapter was vacated and stands empty in the current book.
Three ways a member of a court puts his disagreement on the record, and the thirty-day window for filing.
Transfer of members between churches, associate members, dismissal of ministers, the life of a certificate, and assignment after divestiture.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.t: The Principles and Elements of Public Worship
map.s: Worship is shaped by Scripture alone; it is a meeting of God with his people; no fixed forms are prescribed, and the elements are listed.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.t: The Sanctification of the Lord’s Day
map.s: The whole day is kept holy in public and private exercises of religion, prepared for beforehand.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: The congregation gathers on time, in reverence, and families are encouraged to worship together.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.t: The Public Reading of the Holy Scriptures
map.s: Reading by the minister is God addressing his people; it is read from a good translation, not a paraphrase.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.t: The Singing of Psalms and Hymns
map.s: Praise in song is a duty and privilege; psalms are recommended alongside hymns, and a choir is not to displace the congregation.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: The parts of a full prayer before the sermon, the minister’s duty to prepare, and prayer in the language of the people.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: The text carries the doctrine, sermons are prepared with care and plainness, and no one preaches without the Session’s consent.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.t: The Worship of God by Offerings
map.s: God owns all and we are stewards; giving at least a tithe is part of acknowledging it, in regular and proportionate offerings.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: It is proper for the congregation to confess the faith publicly with creeds true to the Word.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: Baptism by a minister in the presence of the congregation under the Session, with instruction, parental vows and the mode of pouring or sprinkling. Carries full constitutional authority.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.t: The Admission of Persons to Sealing Ordinances
map.s: The Session judges readiness, unbaptized applicants profess and are baptized, and those admitted take five membership vows. Carries full constitutional authority.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.t: The Administration of the Lord’s Supper
map.s: Frequency is set by the Session, the ignorant and scandalous are not admitted, and the invitation follows one of two patterns. Carries full constitutional authority.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: Marriage is a divine institution though not a sacrament, and is only between one man and one woman. Section 59-3 carries full constitutional authority.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: Prayer for the sick, notice to the minister or an officer, and the pastor’s duty and discretion in visiting.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: Psalms or hymns, Scripture with remarks, and prayer for the bereaved, with the service left largely to the minister.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: Who may appoint such days, from families up to the General Assembly, and how they are to be kept.

map.part: Directory for the Worship of God
map.s: Secret worship and family worship as duties, with parents teaching and setting an example.
