glossary.d: The lightest censure: a formal reproof by a court warning an offender of his guilt and danger.
The transfer of a judicial case, after judgment, to the next higher court. Only the party against whom the decision went may appeal.
A believer living away from his permanent home who joins a church without leaving his home church. He may not vote in congregational meetings or hold office.
A pastor elected by the congregation and a member of the Session. His relation to the church is determined by the congregation.
A pastor called by the Session with presbytery’s approval. He is not a member of the Session and his relation is determined by the Session.
Godly men and women appointed by a Session to help the deacons care for those in need. They are not officers and are not ordained.
The part of the Constitution containing the Form of Government, the Rules of Discipline and the Directory for Worship.
A communicant member who believes himself called to preach and submits himself to a presbytery’s care and guidance during his preparation.
A judgment of a court on an offender. The five censures are admonition, suspension from the sacraments, excommunication, suspension from office and deposition.
The written summons issued by order of a court calling an accused person or a witness to appear.
The standard under which a higher court may overturn a lower court’s finding of fact or its judgment on matters that turn on personal knowledge of the parties.
A body authorized to deliberate on and conclude the business referred to it, unlike a committee, which examines and reports.
A committee of the Assembly’s own commissioners through which business ordinarily reaches the floor.
A person who has professed faith in Christ, has been baptized and has been admitted by the Session to the Lord’s Table.
A written representation against an act or decision of a court, open to any communing member in good standing who is subject to that court.
Refusal to obey a citation, to plead, or otherwise to cooperate with lawful proceedings. It draws immediate suspension.
An assembly of presbyters exercising joint jurisdiction: a Session, a presbytery or the General Assembly.
An ordinary and perpetual officer whose work is sympathy and service, including the care of the needy and of church property, under the Session.
Suspension from office for a stated period, used when the offender has satisfied the court as to repentance but the honor of Christ still requires it.
The degrading of an officer from his office, which may or may not carry other censure with it.

glossary.t: Directory for the Worship of God
glossary.d: The third part of the Book of Church Order. It is an approved guide, except that chapters 56, 57 and 58 and section 59-3 have full constitutional authority.
A recorded declaration by a member of the minority that his opinion differs from the court’s action, with reasons if he wishes.
The removal of office from a minister who lacks acceptance in the church, by two-thirds of presbytery, without a finding of guilt.
The officer, in two orders, who governs and oversees the church. Bishop, pastor, presbyter and teacher name one office, not grades.
The designation of a ruling elder or deacon released for age or infirmity, who may attend and speak at meetings but not vote.
Removal of a name from the roll as an act of pastoral discipline without process, after willful neglect and warning.
A teaching elder commissioned for a renewable term of twelve months where there are no PCA churches nearby or in foreign countries, with added powers by separate action of presbytery.
The cutting off of an offender from the communion of the church, used only for gross crime or heresy in one who is incorrigible and contumacious.
A declared difference with the Confession or Catechisms that a court judges may be allowed because it is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion.
The highest court, which represents all the churches in one body and is a permanent court meeting at least annually.
A heresy or immorality considered apart from any wrong to a particular person.
The designation of a minister who wishes to retire by reason of age. He keeps his membership in presbytery and may serve on committees or commissions.
Suspension from the sacraments or from office, without a set end, laid on an impenitent offender until he shows repentance.
The setting of an already ordained officer into a particular charge, without repeating ordination.
A trial period of at least one year, set and supervised by presbytery, in which a candidate’s gifts for ministry are tested.
The joint power of a court to judge. Each court has exclusive original jurisdiction over matters belonging to it, subject to review and control above.
The authority committed to church officers to shut the kingdom against the impenitent by the Word and censures and to open it to penitent sinners.
A man licensed by a presbytery to preach within its bounds. The license runs four years and may be renewed.
The character of all church power: courts serve and declare the law of Christ found in Scripture; they do not make laws that bind the conscience.
A congregation with no permanent governing body, supervised by others, whose goal is to be organized as a particular church.
The officer who presides in a court, with authority to preserve order and conduct business. The pastor moderates his Session by virtue of office.
A child of believers, a member of the church by covenant and birth, entitled to baptism, oversight, instruction and government.
A recorded declaration by a member of a court who had no right to vote on an appeal or complaint but differs from the decision.
Anything in the doctrine or practice of a professing member that is contrary to the Word of God, proved from Scripture as the Standards expound it.
The authoritative admission of a duly called man to office, with prayer and the laying on of hands, and only to a definite work.
The right first to hear and determine a case: presbytery for ministers, the Session for members, with narrow exceptions.
Ordinarily the request of a presbytery for action by the General Assembly on a specific matter.
The equal standing of elders in one office. Ruling elders have the same authority and eligibility in the courts as teaching elders.
A congregation of professing Christians with their children, associated for worship and godly living and submitting to the government of Christ’s kingdom.
A violation of God’s law considered as a wrong or injury to a particular person, which ordinarily requires private steps before prosecution.
Power exercised jointly by officers in courts, after the form of judgment.
Power exercised by officers severally, as in preaching, administering the sacraments, reproving, visiting and comforting.
The court made up of the teaching elders and churches within its bounds. When it meets as a court it comprises teaching elders and ruling elders elected by Sessions.
An offense known only to a few, as distinct from a public offense, which is notorious.
The representative of the Church in a case of process, either a voluntary prosecutor or one appointed by the court, and always a member of the court except in some Session cases.
A more solemn and formal declaration by a minority bearing testimony against what it deems an improper or erroneous action.
The committee elected by a congregation to seek and recommend a pastoral candidate.
The charges, answer, citations and returns, minutes and recordings that a lower court sends up. A higher court considers nothing outside it without consent.
A written application by a lower court asking a higher court for advice or for action on a matter still pending below.
The mode by which a higher court examines the records and proceedings of the court below and requires correction.
An elder, not a minister of the Word, furnished by Christ with gifts and commission to govern, with the same authority in the courts as a teaching elder.
The Assembly’s own operating rules. They are printed with the Book of Church Order but are not part of the Constitution.
The court of a particular church: the pastor, associate pastors and ruling elders, in which the church’s jurisdiction is lodged.
The teaching that the church’s power is exclusively spiritual and its courts have no jurisdiction in political or civil affairs. The phrase is not in the text; the doctrine is.
The Assembly’s commission of twenty-four elders to which all matters under the Rules of Discipline are committed, except the annual review of presbytery records.
The clerk elected by a court to record its transactions, preserve its records and grant extracts, which stand as evidence in every court.
A temporary relation between a church and a minister where no pastor can be secured, for no longer than a year at a time.
An elder specially gifted, called and trained to preach, who also administers the sacraments and holds his membership in presbytery.
The provision in the PC(USA) Book of Order holding congregational property in trust for that denomination. The PCA has no such clause.
All those throughout the world who profess the true religion, together with their children, in every age of redemptive history.

cases.t: A meeting with too few elders
cases.sc: Church A has a pastor and three ruling elders. One elder is travelling. The pastor and one ruling elder meet, receive two new members by profession of faith, and record the action. A week later a member asks whether the reception was valid.

q.q: Was the meeting a quorum?
q.a: Yes. Where a church has fewer than four ruling elders, the pastor and one ruling elder are a quorum, unless the Session has fixed a larger quorum for itself by majority vote.

q.q: Could the same two men have met if the pastor were the one travelling?
q.a: Not as a regular meeting. Without the pastor, a church with fewer than five ruling elders needs two ruling elders, and in an emergency requiring immediate action the Session may elect one of its members to preside, the quorum being the same as for a church with no pastor.

q.q: Was receiving members a proper act for that meeting?
q.a: Yes. Receiving members into the communion of the church is among the Session’s powers, and the reception should appear in the records that go up to presbytery once a year.

cases.sc: During the nomination period at Church B, several communicant members submit the name of a woman who has led the congregation’s mercy work for years. The Session must answer them.

q.q: May the Session place her name before the congregation?
q.a: No. The offices of elder and deacon are open to men only, and each prospective officer should be an active male member who meets the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1.

q.q: What may the Session do instead?
q.a: It may select and appoint godly men and women of the congregation to assist the deacons in caring for the sick, widows, orphans, prisoners and others in distress or need. Such assistants are not officers and are not subjects for ordination.

q.q: May she be given the title of deacon or deaconess in the bulletin?
q.a: No. Unordained people are not to be referred to as, or given the titles of, the ordained offices of pastor, elder or deacon.

cases.sc: Church C has 260 communing members. Fifty-two of them sign a written request asking the Session to call a congregational meeting to consider a building project. Forty days pass and the Session neither calls the meeting nor answers.

q.q: Was the request sufficient?
q.a: Yes. In a church of more than 100 and not more than 300 communing members, a fifth of them may require the Session to call a meeting. A fifth of 260 is 52.

q.q: What may the signers do now?
q.a: Where the Session cannot act, fails to act or refuses to act within thirty days of a proper request, any member or members in good standing may file a complaint.

q.q: Where is that complaint filed, and by when?
q.a: First with the clerk of the Session itself, in writing with supporting reasons, within sixty days following the meeting whose action or failure is complained of. If the Session denies it, notice goes to the clerks of both courts within thirty days of notification.

cases.t: A wrong that one member did another
cases.sc: Member D believes member E has slandered him. He has said nothing to E, but comes to the Session asking that charges be brought.

q.q: May D become the prosecutor?
q.a: Not yet. An injured party may not become the prosecutor of a personal offense without first trying the means of reconciliation and of reclaiming the offender that Christ requires in Matthew 18.

q.q: Can the Session act at all before those steps are taken?
q.a: It may. A court may judicially investigate a personal offense as if it were general when the interest of religion seems to demand it, and it has a standing duty to require satisfactory explanations concerning reports affecting a member’s Christian character.

q.q: If process does begin, who is the accuser?
q.a: The Presbyterian Church in America, whose honour and purity are to be maintained. The prosecutor, whether voluntary or appointed, represents the church.

cases.t: A candidate with a stated difference
cases.sc: A candidate before presbytery states that he differs with the Confession on one point and describes the difference in his own words. The examination is otherwise satisfactory.

q.q: What must presbytery decide?
q.a: Whether the declared difference is out of accord with a fundamental of the system of doctrine. An exception may be granted only if the difference is neither hostile to the system nor strikes at the vitals of religion.

q.q: What must the minutes record?
q.a: The stated difference in the man’s own words, and which of four findings the court made: no differences; merely semantic; more than semantic but not out of accord; or out of accord, that is hostile to the system or striking at the vitals of religion.

q.q: If he later changes his view on another article, what is required of him?
q.a: The second ordination vow binds him to make the change known to his presbytery on his own initiative.

cases.t: Counting the days on a complaint
cases.sc: A Session acts at its stated meeting on June 1. A member files a written complaint with the clerk on July 20. The Session considers the complaint at a meeting on August 10 and denies it, notifying the complainant by hand delivery on August 12.

q.q: Was the complaint filed in time?
q.a: Yes. Written notice with supporting reasons must be filed with the clerk within sixty days following the meeting. July 20 is within sixty days of June 1.

q.q: Was the Session obliged to consider it on August 10?
q.a: It must consider the complaint at its next stated meeting, or a called meeting before then, provided the complaint was filed at least ten days in advance. Filed July 20, the complaint met that requirement.

q.q: What is the deadline for carrying the complaint to presbytery?
q.a: Thirty days from notification, which here means September 11, with written notice filed with the clerk of the Session and the clerk of presbytery.

cases.t: The associate who is asked to stay
cases.sc: The pastor of Church F resigns and the relation is dissolved. The congregation wants its associate pastor to become the pastor without his serving elsewhere first.

q.q: Is that ordinarily allowed?
q.a: No. An associate or assistant may continue to serve when the senior pastor’s relation is dissolved, but may not normally succeed him without an intervening term of service in a different field of labour.

q.q: What would an exception require?
q.a: A petition to presbytery adopted by the congregation on secret ballot with a four-fifths majority, which presbytery may grant by a three-fourths majority.

q.q: What must presbytery weigh before granting it?
q.a: Whether the dissolution of the pastoral relationship with the senior pastor was brought about in Christian love and good order on the part of the parties concerned.

cases.sc: Church G is considering leaving the denomination. The Session asks what the book requires, and what happens to the building.

q.q: What notice is required?
q.a: At least thirty days notice to the congregation of the meeting at which the withdrawal is to be voted.

q.q: Who owns the property?
q.a: The congregation, through its corporation officers or trustees. All particular churches are entitled to hold, own and enjoy their own local properties without any right of reversion to any court, and chapter 25 is framed as a solemn covenant that the church will never try to take a congregation’s property against its will.

q.q: Would the answer be the same in the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.)?
q.a: No. There all property held by or for a congregation is held in trust for the denomination, and a congregation’s relationship to the denomination may be severed only by constitutional action of the presbytery.

cases.sc: Teaching elder H has been on the roll of his presbytery without a call for three years. He files his annual reports, but presbytery judges that he lacks acceptance in the church.

q.q: What does the book require presbytery to do?
q.a: A minister may not be continued on the roll without a call for a prolonged period beyond three years without following the procedure of 34-10, and presbytery must inquire at a stated meeting into the cause of habitual failure to discharge official functions.

q.q: What may presbytery decide?
q.a: Where the neglect proceeds only from lack of acceptance in the church, presbytery may divest him of office without censure, even against his will, by a two-thirds majority.

q.q: What protects him?
q.a: Written notice from the clerk, delivered before the next stated meeting, distinctly stating the grounds; a hearing in his own defense; and a right of appeal as if he had been tried in the usual form. If divested, presbytery assigns him to membership in a particular church, subject to that Session’s approval.

cases.t: A confession offered to the Session
cases.sc: Ruling elder J comes to his Session, confesses a specific sin against a named member, and asks the Session to deal with him without a trial.

q.q: What must be in place before judgment?
q.a: A written confession containing a sufficient summary of the facts, his specific confession, and any expression or evidence of repentance, approved by him and by the court, and appended to the minutes when co-signed.

q.q: What is owed to the person he wronged?
q.a: The court must try to inform that person of the part of the confession it deems pertinent, invite comment before final approval, encourage the person to enlist an advisor, and report how the offended were informed.

q.q: If the Session censures him, may he appeal?
q.a: Yes. Those appealing a censure in a case without process are among the parties entitled to appeal, and he may be assisted by a representative.

cases.t: An appeal that asks for a different verdict
cases.sc: After a trial, a Session finds a member guilty, resting on its judgment that one witness was more believable than another. The member appeals to presbytery, arguing that the Session weighed the witnesses wrongly and also misread a section of the book.

q.q: How will presbytery treat the credibility question?
q.a: With great deference. Comparative credibility of conflicting witnesses is named among the matters of discretion and judgment that only a court with familiar acquaintance of the events and parties can address, and it will not be reversed unless there is clear error.

q.q: How will it treat the reading of the book?
q.a: Without deference. On the interpretation of the Constitution the higher court has the duty and authority to interpret and apply according to its best ability and understanding, whatever the lower court thought.

q.q: What may presbytery do with the case?
q.a: Affirm in whole or in part, reverse in whole or in part, render the decision that should have been rendered, or remand for a new trial, in every case with a written opinion.

cases.sc: A visiting family asks whether they may commune at Church K. Two elders disagree: one thinks all professing believers in good standing elsewhere may come, the other thinks the Session should approve people in advance.

q.q: Which elder is right?
q.a: Both describe a lawful practice. At the Session’s discretion the minister may either invite all who profess the true religion and are communicants in good standing in any evangelical church, or invite those whom the Session has approved after they have indicated their desire to participate.

q.q: Who decides between them?
q.a: The Session, which also determines how often the Supper is observed and exercises authority over the time and place of the Sacraments.

q.q: Is there anyone the book excludes?
q.a: Yes. The ignorant and the scandalous are not to be admitted to the Lord’s Supper.

processes.d: The path a change takes, and where it can stop.

steps.b: Ordinarily a presbytery adopts the request and sends it to the Assembly. Presbytery has power to propose measures of common advantage to the church at large.

The stated clerk refers overtures seeking amendment of the book or the Assembly’s rules to the Committee on Constitutional Business for advice, and overtures proposing amendment of the Constitution to the Overtures Committee. The referral is final unless the Assembly redirects it.
A majority of those present and voting approves the proposed amendment to the Book of Church Order and recommends it to the presbyteries. For the Confession or Catechisms, three-fourths is required.

Two-thirds of presbyteries must give advice and consent for the Book of Church Order; three-fourths for the doctrinal standards. Presbyteries may not divide the parts of an amendment except as the Assembly directs.
A subsequent Assembly approves and enacts, by majority for the book and by three-fourths for the standards. Where too few presbyteries have reported, the Assembly may defer for a year.

processes.d: Every gate between a man’s first application and his installation.

steps.b: He applies to the presbytery with jurisdiction over his church, with his Session’s endorsement, after at least six months membership. He is examined on experiential religion and motives, answers two questions and is enrolled as a candidate.

Examined in Christian experience and inward call, basic knowledge of doctrine, Bible content and church government, with a sermon on an assigned passage; states any differences with the standards; answers four questions; licensed for four years.

At least one year under presbytery’s supervision, in the full scope of ministerial duties. He may not administer the Sacraments. At the end it is approved or disapproved. Equivalent experience may be approved by a three-fourths vote.

A written call to definite work, ordinarily from a church, presbytery or the Assembly, with financial arrangements and assurance of liberty to preach the whole counsel of God, placed in his hands by presbytery.

Diplomas or their equivalent; examination in experiential religion and character, original languages, Bible content, theology, the Sacraments, church history, the history of this church, and government and discipline; a thesis; an exegesis; a sermon. Omissions require three-fourths with reasons recorded.
Sermon, recital of the proceedings, the ordination questions, the congregation’s questions, prayer with the laying on of the hands of presbytery, the right hand of fellowship, declaration and charge.

processes.t: Electing a ruling elder or deacon
processes.d: From the Session’s call for names to the laying on of hands.

steps.b: At times the Session determines, communicant members submit names, keeping the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 in view.

Nominees are instructed in the qualifications and work of the office, then examined in Christian experience and character, Bible content, the system of doctrine, government and discipline, the duties of the office, and willingness to assent to the ordination questions.
The Session reports those found eligible and gives at least thirty days notice of the congregational meeting. It may judge a man ineligible on Christian experience at any point in the process.

Communing members in good and regular standing vote; a majority of votes cast, excluding blanks and abstentions, elects. If a large minority is averse, the moderator seeks to dissuade the majority, but the election stands if the majority insists.

A sermon, a statement of the office, the questions to the candidate, the congregation’s question, prayer with the laying on of the hands of the Session, the right hand of fellowship, declaration and exhortation.

processes.d: What a vacant church does, in order.

steps.b: The Session calls a congregational meeting to elect a pulpit committee, drawn from the congregation at large or the Session as the congregation designates.
After consultation and deliberation the committee recommends a candidate who meets the constitutional requirements of the office and is best suited to the congregation’s spiritual interests.
Ordered by the Session at the regular place of worship, with public notice of time, place and purpose at least one week before. A minister or ruling elder of this church presides if practicable.
Communing members in good and regular standing vote; a majority of votes cast, excluding blanks and abstentions, elects. A large minority is addressed under 20-5 before the call is pressed.
The moderator draws the call in due form, certifies the number not concurring and any facts of importance, and commissioners present and prosecute the call before presbytery.

Presbytery may recommend that the congregation desist, place the call in the man’s hands with or without advice, or decline to place it. A minister coming from another presbytery must be examined and received, and released by his own presbytery.

processes.d: How a personal wrong becomes a judicial case, and where it should stop.

steps.b: The individual’s responsibility to admonish. Instruction in the Word comes first, and the steps must be followed in proper order.
If admonition is rejected, the calling of one or more witnesses.
If rejection persists, the church acts through her court. An injured party may not prosecute a personal offense without having tried these means first.
The court demands satisfactory explanations concerning reports affecting Christian character. If a strong presumption of guilt appears, it institutes process and appoints a prosecutor.

The charge is reduced to writing. At the first meeting the court appoints a prosecutor, orders the indictment drawn and served with the names of known witnesses, and cites the accused to appear not sooner than ten days later.
At the second meeting the charges are read and the accused pleads. If he takes issue, the trial is set not sooner than fourteen days after citation and follows the six-step order of 32-15.

The vote is taken, the verdict announced and judgment entered. Admonition or definite suspension concludes the process where the offender satisfies the court as to repentance; indefinite suspension or excommunication follows impenitence.

processes.d: The route for a member who believes a court acted wrongly.

steps.t: Check that complaint is the right remedy
steps.b: Any communing member in good standing subject to the court may complain against any action of it. No complaint is allowable in a judicial case after process has commenced, though one filed then is held until the case ends.

steps.t: File with the court complained against
steps.b: Written notice with supporting reasons, filed with that court’s clerk within sixty days following the meeting.
At its next stated meeting, or a called meeting before then, provided the complaint was filed at least ten days in advance.
Written notice filed with the clerks of both courts within thirty days of notification of the decision. The same route is open if the lower court fails to consider it.

Notice does not suspend the action unless a third of those present when it was taken so vote. The court complained against appoints representatives; the parties are complainant and respondent; the complainant opens and closes the argument.
The higher court may annul the whole or part of the action, or send the matter back with instructions for a new hearing.

processes.d: The route for a party against whom judgment was rendered.

steps.b: Appeal is open to those who submitted to a regular trial, those censured in a case without process, those whose censure was raised under 36-8, and those divested without censure under 34-10.
Notice may be given before the court adjourns. Written notice with supporting reasons is filed with the clerks of both courts within thirty days of notification.
The clerk of the lower court files the Record of the Case within thirty days of receiving notice. Nothing outside the Record is considered without the consent of the parties.

The judgment is suspended, though the court of original jurisdiction may, for recorded reasons and by a two-thirds vote, keep the appellant from the Table or from official functions, never as censure.
After the Record is read, each side has not over thirty minutes, the appellant opening and closing. The court votes on each specification of error in turn.
Affirm in whole or part, reverse in whole or part, render the decision that should have been rendered, or remand for a new trial, always with a written opinion.

processes.d: From a gathering under supervision to a constituted church.

steps.b: On its own initiative, at a Session’s initiative, or on the written petition of an independent gathering. Outside presbytery bounds, an Assembly committee may exercise these powers.
An evangelist, or a mother church Session, or a commission serving as a temporary Session, with records submitted to presbytery for annual review.
Under chapter 57 so far as it applies. Those received are communing or non-communing members of this church, and rolls are kept separately.

When qualified men appear, nomination and election follow chapter 24 so far as it applies, normally at least two weeks before the organization service, with the new officers taking office at its completion.
The members sign a petition to presbytery. On approval, presbytery appoints an organizing commission and sets the date and time of the service.
Officers are ordained and installed, a pastor may be ordained or installed, the members enter into covenant with uplifted hand, and the commission declares them constituted a church.

steps.t: First acts of the new Session
steps.b: Elect a stated clerk, form a budget, and where there is no pastor elect a moderator and act to secure the regular administration of Word and Sacraments.
